one_line_idea: Entropy-minimization test-time adaptation gains are specialized to synthetic corruption-style shifts and vanish or reverse on natural distribution shifts.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time adaptation methods based on entropy minimization are predominantly developed and validated on synthetic corruption suites, yet they are marketed as general robustness tools for deployment shift.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The unlabeled-adaptation signal exploited by entropy minimization is only reliable when the shift preserves class-conditional structure the way synthetic corruptions do, so gains fail to transfer to natural shifts such as geographic, temporal, or population change.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A matched evaluation of entropy-minimization adaptation on synthetic corruption shifts versus natural shifts of comparable severity will show positive gains on the former and near-zero or negative gains on a substantial fraction of the latter.
why_important: If adaptation methods only work on the shift family they were tuned on, deploying them on real drift can silently degrade models, which is worse than not adapting at all.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual failure anecdotes exist, but a systematic shift-family transfer matrix for test-time adaptation, with severity matched across shift families, may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one public vision backbone, apply one standard entropy-minimization adaptation method, and evaluate the same pipeline on a synthetic corruption suite and on natural-shift test sets, comparing adaptation gain by shift family at matched baseline degradation.
main_risk: Matching shift severity across families is nontrivial; if severity is confounded with family, the comparison could be attributed to difficulty rather than shift type.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community broadly treats gains on corruption suites as evidence that a test-time adaptation method improves robustness to distribution shift in general.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Corruptions change marginal input statistics while keeping semantics fixed, which is exactly the regime where confidence sharpening is safe; natural shifts change semantics and priors, breaking that safety.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, one entropy-minimization method, two corruption types and two natural-shift test sets, one afternoon of GPU inference, compare signed adaptation gains.

one_line_idea: Most published test-time adaptation gains are batch-statistics artifacts that disappear at batch size one, the realistic streaming regime.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many test-time adaptation methods recompute normalization statistics or optimize objectives over large test batches, while real deployments often see one image at a time.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large share of reported adaptation gain comes from batch-level statistics estimation rather than from any learned adaptation, so gains shrink monotonically with batch size and approach zero at single-sample streaming.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping test batch size from large to one for several published adaptation methods will show gains collapsing toward the unadapted baseline, with method rankings at batch size one differing from rankings at large batch size.
why_important: Deployment scenarios that motivate test-time adaptation, such as robots and mobile devices, are exactly the ones that cannot form large i.i.d. test batches, so the evaluation regime contradicts the use case.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Batch-size sensitivity has been noted for individual methods, but a unified batch-size scaling curve across method families, treated as a primary evaluation axis rather than an ablation, may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-run several public adaptation methods with identical settings while sweeping only the test batch size, and plot adaptation gain versus batch size per method and shift.
main_risk: Some methods have explicit single-sample variants, so the claim must be scoped to the evaluation protocols actually used in the literature rather than to the best possible variant.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Batch size is widely regarded as an implementation detail of test-time adaptation rather than the causal source of its benefit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Normalization-statistic correction is known to be a strong corruption baseline on its own, which suggests batch statistics, not parameter learning, carry much of the observed effect.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, one corruption suite, batch sizes from two hundred down to one on a single GPU, check whether gain at batch size one is within noise of zero.

one_line_idea: Test-time adaptation hyperparameters are implicitly tuned on the test distribution, making reported gains circular; shift-blind hyperparameter selection erases most of them.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time adaptation has no labeled validation data by definition, yet published methods report specific learning rates, momentum values, and update schedules that vary per benchmark.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The published hyperparameters encode oracle knowledge of the test shift, and under a rigorous protocol where hyperparameters must be fixed before seeing the shift, most methods lose most of their advantage over the unadapted baseline.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Selecting each method's hyperparameters on one shift family and deploying them unchanged on a different shift family will reduce average gains substantially and cause negative gains for some method-shift pairs.
why_important: If gains require knowing the shift in advance, the methods do not solve the stated problem, since knowing the shift in advance would allow far stronger interventions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Oracle model selection has been criticized in domain generalization, but an equivalent formal audit for the test-time adaptation literature, with cross-shift hyperparameter transfer as the headline protocol, may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a shift-blind protocol where hyperparameters are chosen on held-out synthetic shifts only, then evaluate several published methods on disjoint shift families and compare to their published-configuration results.
main_risk: Some gains may be genuinely hyperparameter-insensitive, so the audit must report per-method sensitivity rather than a single aggregate to avoid overclaiming.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Readers generally assume reported test-time adaptation gains would survive honest hyperparameter selection because the methods are described as unsupervised.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Unsupervised objectives like entropy are known to be unstable to learning-rate choice, and instability plus per-benchmark tuning is the classic signature of oracle selection.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take two published methods, swap their per-benchmark hyperparameters across benchmarks, and check whether gains survive the swap on one backbone in a day.

one_line_idea: Core test-time adaptation conclusions were formed on batch-normalized convolutional networks and do not transfer to layer-normalized transformer foundation models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Much of the test-time adaptation literature builds on updating batch-normalization statistics or affine parameters, while modern vision foundation models predominantly use layer normalization without batch-level statistics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The mechanism, stability properties, and method rankings of test-time adaptation change qualitatively when the backbone is a layer-normalized transformer, so a substantial portion of accepted best practice is architecture-era-specific rather than general.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-running a representative set of adaptation methods on a transformer foundation-model backbone will change method rankings relative to convolutional results and show different failure modes, such as sensitivity concentrated in early normalization layers.
why_important: Practitioners applying published adaptation recipes to foundation models may inherit advice that is not just suboptimal but actively harmful for their architecture class.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual papers evaluate transformers, but a deliberate era-transfer audit asking which convolutional-era adaptation conclusions survive on foundation-model backbones may not have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a shift benchmark, run the same set of adaptation methods on one convolutional and one transformer backbone of comparable baseline accuracy, and compare rankings, gains, and collapse rates.
main_risk: Backbones differ in pretraining data as well as architecture, so attributing differences to normalization type requires controlling for pretraining as far as public checkpoints allow.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community treats test-time adaptation methods as backbone-agnostic wrappers that can be applied to any model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Several methods literally operate on batch-statistics modules that transformers do not have, so architecture independence is impossible at the mechanism level.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One corruption suite, two backbones, three methods, compare signed gains and rank order within a day of GPU time.

one_line_idea: Under long unlabeled streams, most self-supervised test-time adaptation methods eventually collapse to trivial predictions, and collapse frequency is a hidden but decisive metric.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Objectives like entropy minimization admit degenerate optima where the model predicts a single class with high confidence, and test-time adaptation is typically evaluated on short episodes that end before degeneracy can develop.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Collapse is not an edge case but the asymptotic behavior of most unsupervised adaptation objectives, so extending evaluation horizon by one to two orders of magnitude will reveal widespread collapse that current protocols never measure.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Running published methods on streams extended well beyond standard episode lengths will show a large fraction of method-shift pairs entering measurable prediction-diversity collapse, with time-to-collapse varying by orders of magnitude across methods.
why_important: A deployed adapter that collapses after a week is worse than no adapter, and the field currently has no standard measurement of this risk.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Collapse is acknowledged qualitatively in some papers, but time-to-collapse as a quantitative, reported metric with standardized long-horizon streams may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct long stationary and non-stationary unlabeled streams from existing shift datasets by resampling, run each method until prediction entropy over classes degenerates or the stream ends, and report time-to-collapse distributions.
main_risk: Resampled long streams may repeat images, and repetition itself could either accelerate or mask collapse relative to genuinely fresh data.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners assume regularizers and small learning rates make collapse rare enough to ignore in practice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Degenerate optima are global attractors of the objective itself, so regularization changes the timescale of collapse rather than removing the attractor.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method known to be aggressive, one shift, a stream one hundred times the standard length by cycling data, watch class-marginal entropy over time in a few GPU-hours.

one_line_idea: A frozen foundation model with a test-time nearest-neighbor or retrieval-augmented classifier matches gradient-based test-time adaptation at far lower risk.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Gradient-based test-time adaptation mutates model parameters on unlabeled data, which introduces collapse and drift risk, while nonparametric classifiers over frozen features can also absorb test-distribution information without touching weights.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Accumulating test embeddings in a memory and classifying by neighborhood vote or prototype update captures most of the benefit that parameter-updating adaptation achieves, because the useful adaptation signal is a shift in feature-space class geometry rather than in the features themselves.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On standard adaptation benchmarks with a strong frozen backbone, a memory-based nonparametric adapter will reach a large fraction of the gain of gradient-based methods while never degrading below the zero-shot baseline on any tested shift.
why_important: If true, deployments get most of the robustness benefit with a mechanism that is trivially reversible, auditable, and immune to weight collapse.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prototype and memory ideas exist in the literature, but a head-to-head risk-versus-gain comparison framing nonparametric adaptation as a safety-dominant substitute for gradient adaptation on foundation models may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement a streaming prototype or nearest-neighbor head over a frozen public backbone, compare against two gradient-based methods on the same shifts, and report both average gain and worst-case degradation.
main_risk: Memory-based methods depend on class balance in the stream, and heavily skewed streams could poison prototypes in a way that mirrors gradient collapse.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The field treats parameter updating as the substantive form of adaptation and nonparametric heads as weak baselines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With strong pretrained features, most shift-induced error is arguably in the classifier geometry, which is exactly the part a nonparametric head can fix without gradients.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, one shift suite, streaming prototype head versus one entropy-minimization method, compare gain and worst-case drop in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Most of what test-time adaptation improves is calibration and decision thresholds, not representation quality, and a post-hoc output correction recovers the bulk of its accuracy gain.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time adaptation methods update internal parameters and report accuracy improvements under shift, but the mechanism of improvement is rarely decomposed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant effect of popular adaptation methods is equivalent to a shift-conditional rescaling and re-prioring of the output distribution, so a purely post-hoc correction that estimates test-class marginals and temperature achieves most of the same accuracy gain without touching features.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across several methods and shifts, an output-layer-only correction pipeline will recover a majority of the accuracy gain of full adaptation, and the residual gain attributable to feature change will be small and shift-dependent.
why_important: If gains live in the output layer, the field can replace risky weight surgery with cheap, transparent probability corrections and redirect research toward the genuinely hard residual.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mechanistic decompositions of where adaptation gains come from, separating output recalibration from representation change with matched-budget baselines, appear rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For each method and shift, fit a label-marginal and temperature correction on the same unlabeled test data the method uses, compare accuracy gains, and measure feature-space movement to correlate residual gains with representation change.
main_risk: Estimating test-class marginals without labels is itself error-prone, and a weak estimator could understate how much of the gain is output-level.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adaptation is assumed to repair internal representations damaged by shift, which is why parameter updates are considered necessary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Entropy-style objectives act most directly on logit sharpness and class priors, so the output-level interpretation matches the objective's actual gradient structure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, three shifts, compare entropy-minimization gain to an unlabeled temperature-plus-prior correction on the same test batches in a day.

one_line_idea: Test-time adaptation methods are doing implicit label-shift estimation, and explicit unlabeled class-prior correction matches them whenever the shift includes a prior change.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real-world shifts usually mix covariate change with label-prior change, and classical label-shift correction methods estimate test priors from unlabeled data under known conditions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A significant fraction of test-time adaptation benefit on realistic shifts is attributable to implicit prior correction, so on shifts constructed to have pure prior change, explicit classical estimators will match or beat gradient-based adaptation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On label-shift-only test sets built by resampling class frequencies, classical prior-correction will equal or exceed popular adaptation methods, while on covariate-only shifts the ordering will reverse, producing a diagnostic two-axis profile per method.
why_important: Decomposing adaptation gains into prior versus covariate components tells practitioners which cheap tool to deploy and exposes what current methods actually do.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label-shift literature and test-time adaptation literature are largely disjoint, and a controlled factorial comparison across pure-prior, pure-covariate, and mixed shifts may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build three shift conditions from one dataset by resampling priors, applying input corruptions, and combining both, then compare classical prior correction, gradient adaptation, and their composition on each condition.
main_risk: Pure conditions are idealized, and interaction effects in the mixed condition may dominate in practice, limiting what the factorial design reveals.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Test-time adaptation is framed as covariate-shift repair, and label-prior change is treated as a separate niche problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Entropy minimization provably responds to class-marginal skew in the test batch, so prior adaptation is built into the objective whether or not it is acknowledged.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One dataset, resample to three skewed prior settings without any input change, run one adaptation method versus classical prior correction, half a day.

one_line_idea: Single-sample adaptation methods built on augmentation consistency mostly repackage test-time augmentation ensembling, and the learning component adds little.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Several single-sample adaptation methods minimize the entropy of the averaged prediction over augmented views of one test image, which entangles two mechanisms: augmentation ensembling and parameter update.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The augmentation-averaged prediction alone, with no parameter update, captures the majority of the reported gain, so the gradient step contributes a minor and sometimes negative residual.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] An ablation comparing full method, augmentation-ensemble-only, and update-only variants will show the ensemble-only variant within a small margin of the full method across most shifts.
why_important: If ensembling drives the gain, the compute story changes completely, since ensembling is parallelizable and stateless while updates are sequential and risky.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The specific decomposition of single-sample adaptation into ensembling and updating contributions, evaluated across the popular methods rather than within one paper's ablation, may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reimplement two or three single-sample adaptation methods with switches to disable the parameter update or the augmentation averaging independently, and report the two-by-two ablation across shift benchmarks.
main_risk: Fair update-only variants require care because the update was designed assuming the averaged objective, and a clumsy ablation could understate the update's role.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The parameter update is presented and perceived as the core contribution of these methods, with augmentation as scaffolding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Test-time augmentation is a decades-old accuracy booster, and objectives selecting confident augmented views inherit exactly that boost before any learning occurs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, one shift suite, run ensemble-only ablation with identical augmentations, compare accuracy in a few GPU-hours.

one_line_idea: No current test-time adaptation method knows when not to adapt; a simple do-no-harm gate based on stream statistics prevents most catastrophic adaptation failures.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time adaptation can degrade accuracy when the test stream is actually in-distribution, adversarial, or too skewed, yet published methods adapt unconditionally on whatever stream they receive.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A lightweight gate that monitors cheap statistics, such as embedding-distribution distance from a pretraining reference and prediction-marginal skew, can decide when to enable adaptation and thereby eliminate the majority of negative-gain episodes while retaining most positive-gain episodes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a suite of helpful and harmful stream conditions, gated adaptation will show near-zero worst-case degradation while ungated adaptation shows large worst-case degradation, at a small cost in average gain.
why_important: Worst-case behavior, not average gain, blocks deployment of self-modifying models; a credible gate converts adaptation from a research demo into a shippable feature.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Safety gating appears in fragments across papers, but a standardized harmful-stream benchmark plus a general-purpose gate evaluated on worst-case metrics may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble stream conditions including in-distribution, mild shift, severe shift, and class-skewed streams, implement the statistical gate in front of two adaptation methods, and compare worst-case and average gains gated versus ungated.
main_risk: A gate tuned on known harmful conditions may fail on unanticipated ones, which is the same generalization problem one level up.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Papers implicitly assume the deployment stream is shifted in a way their method helps, so the decision of whether to adapt is not treated as part of the problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The decision of whether to adapt is a far lower-dimensional problem than how to adapt, so simple statistics plausibly suffice for the gate even when adaptation itself is hard.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One adaptation method, three stream conditions including one in-distribution stream, a two-threshold gate on embedding shift and prediction skew, compare worst-case degradation in a day.

one_line_idea: Periodic hard reset to source weights beats sophisticated anti-forgetting machinery in continual test-time adaptation over long horizons.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Continual test-time adaptation methods add mechanisms like stochastic weight restoration and regularization toward source to prevent drift, adding complexity and hyperparameters.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The entire benefit of these mechanisms is approximated by periodically resetting all adapted parameters to the source checkpoint, because the useful adaptation state is cheap to reacquire while accumulated drift is expensive to undo.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On long non-stationary streams, plain adaptation plus periodic reset will match or exceed dedicated continual-adaptation methods across most shift sequences, for some reset period spanning a wide tolerant range.
why_important: If a one-line baseline matches complex methods, the field's complexity is unjustified and evaluation practice failed to include the obvious control.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Reset appears as an ablation in some papers, but reset-period sweeps positioned as the primary baseline for the continual adaptation literature seem absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run two dedicated continual-adaptation methods and reset-augmented plain adaptation on standard corruption sequences and one natural drift stream, sweeping reset period logarithmically, and compare final and time-averaged accuracy.
main_risk: Reset timing may interact badly with abrupt shift boundaries, and an unlucky fixed period could strawman the baseline unless the sweep is wide.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Forgetting-prevention machinery is considered necessary because naive continual adaptation degrades, and reset is dismissed as wasteful.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptation state for normalization-level updates is reacquired within tens of batches, so the amortized cost of resets is tiny compared to the compounding cost of drift.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One corruption sequence, one continual method versus entropy minimization with three reset periods, compare time-averaged accuracy in a few GPU-hours.

one_line_idea: Episodic reset-per-shift evaluation protocols overstate test-time adaptation practicality, and realistic recurring mixed-shift streams reverse published method rankings.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard protocols evaluate adaptation on one shift at a time, often resetting the model between shifts, while real streams interleave and revisit conditions such as day, night, and weather without announced boundaries.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Method rankings are protocol-dependent, and under unannounced recurring mixed shifts, methods that look strong episodically will underperform simpler or memory-based approaches because their state management assumptions break.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructing streams that interleave and revisit shift conditions will produce method rankings with low rank correlation to episodic-protocol rankings, and at least some published methods will fall below the never-adapt baseline.
why_important: Benchmark protocols function as the field's objective function; if the protocol rewards the wrong behaviors, the literature optimizes for scenarios that do not occur.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Continual adaptation benchmarks exist, but recurring-condition streams with unannounced revisits, explicitly designed to test state reuse, may be an unoccupied evaluation niche.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build recurring mixed streams from existing shift datasets with a hidden condition schedule, evaluate a representative method set, and compare rankings to the episodic protocol on identical underlying data.
main_risk: Stream construction choices such as revisit frequency could themselves determine rankings, so conclusions must be shown stable across schedule randomizations.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Episodic per-shift results are read as predictive of deployment behavior on mixed streams.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Episodic protocols never test whether a method can exploit recurrence or recover from interleaving, which are the dominant structures of real drift.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Interleave two alternating shift conditions into one stream, run three methods, check whether episodic winners still win, one day.

one_line_idea: Test-time prompt tuning gains for vision-language models are mostly attributable to augmentation ensembling and confident-view selection rather than to learned prompt updates.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time prompt tuning methods for vision-language models generate augmented views, filter to confident ones, and update prompt vectors, entangling three mechanisms in one reported gain.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The view-generation and confidence-filtering pipeline is the dominant source of gain, and replacing the learned prompt update with no update, while keeping the filtered-view ensemble prediction, retains most reported improvement.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A component ablation across shifts will show the no-update filtered-ensemble variant within a small margin of the full method, and the prompt-update-only variant close to the zero-shot baseline.
why_important: Prompt updating requires backpropagation through the text encoder at test time; if it is unnecessary, the same robustness is available at a fraction of latency and complexity.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Published ablations exist within individual papers, but an adversarially thorough decomposition across the family of prompt-tuning-at-test-time methods, run by a third party, may not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reimplement one or two test-time prompt tuning methods with independent switches for augmentation ensembling, confidence filtering, and prompt updates, and report the full factorial on standard shift benchmarks.
main_risk: Interaction terms may be real, with updates helping only in combination with filtering, so the factorial rather than one-at-a-time ablation is essential.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The learned prompt update is perceived as the substantive mechanism, since it is the titled contribution of these methods.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Confidence-filtered test-time augmentation is a known strong booster on its own, and one gradient step on a handful of views is a weak learner by comparison.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, one shift benchmark, run the no-update ablation with identical views and filtering, compare in hours.

one_line_idea: Matching test images to the pretraining input-statistics envelope, a trivial input-space normalization, is a stronger and safer baseline than most parameter-updating test-time adaptation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many deployment shifts include low-level statistics changes such as contrast, color balance, blur, and compression, and foundation models were pretrained on data with a particular envelope of such statistics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Estimating simple global statistics of the test stream and transforming inputs toward the pretraining envelope recovers a large share of shift-induced degradation on low-level shifts, matching parameter-updating methods there while being trivially reversible.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On corruption-style and sensor-style shifts, input-statistics matching will achieve a large fraction of the gain of gradient-based adaptation, while on semantic shifts it will do nothing, cleanly separating which published gains are low-level.
why_important: A strong trivial baseline recalibrates the field's sense of progress and gives practitioners a zero-risk first-line tool.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Input normalization appears in older robustness work, but its systematic use as a control baseline for the modern test-time adaptation literature on foundation models may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement channel-statistics and frequency-envelope matching from unlabeled test batches, compare against two adaptation methods across low-level and semantic shift suites on one frozen backbone.
main_risk: Overly aggressive input transforms can destroy task-relevant detail, so the transform family must be constrained and the constraint choice affects results.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Input-space fixes are considered preprocessing hygiene rather than adaptation, and are absent from method comparison tables.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If a shift is literally a change in input statistics, undoing it in input space is the direct solution, and parameter updates are an indirect approximation of the same correction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Histogram-match test images to a small pretraining-like reference set on two corruption types, compare to entropy minimization, a few hours.

one_line_idea: Classical unsupervised domain adaptation methods built for weak backbones add approximately nothing on top of modern foundation-model features.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The unsupervised domain adaptation literature largely predates strong pretrained vision foundation models, and its methods were validated on backbones whose features were far weaker than current ones.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The gap those methods closed was a feature-quality gap, not a fundamental adaptation gap, so with a frozen strong foundation backbone plus simple target-side self-training, adversarial alignment and discrepancy-minimization methods provide no additional benefit.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A re-evaluation of representative alignment-based methods on foundation-model backbones will show their marginal gain over source-only-plus-self-training shrinking to within noise on the majority of standard adaptation tasks.
why_important: If backbone progress dissolved the problem the methods solved, ongoing method development on legacy benchmarks is misallocated effort, and the open problems lie elsewhere.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual observations of shrinking gains exist, but a systematic obsolescence audit of the adaptation method stack under modern backbones, with method families as the unit of analysis, may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix several standard adaptation dataset pairs, run source-only, self-training, and two classical alignment methods on both a legacy backbone and a modern foundation backbone, and compare marginal gains across backbone eras.
main_risk: Fair reimplementation of legacy methods on new architectures is nontrivial, and a weak port could unfairly deflate their measured contribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Alignment objectives are still presented as the core technology of domain adaptation, with the backbone treated as an interchangeable feature extractor.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Foundation features were trained on data spanning enormous visual diversity, so many benchmark domain gaps are plausibly already inside the pretraining envelope where no alignment is needed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One adaptation dataset pair, foundation backbone, source-only versus one adversarial-alignment method versus self-training, compare in a day.

one_line_idea: Marginal feature-alignment objectives actively hurt adaptation when source and target label distributions differ, and popular benchmarks hide this by having nearly matched label marginals.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Aligning marginal feature distributions across domains is provably harmful when label proportions differ, since forcing marginals together must distort class-conditional structure, yet marginal alignment remains a default component.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Standard benchmark pairs have incidentally similar label marginals, which is why the harm is invisible; introducing controlled label-proportion mismatch will make alignment methods underperform source-only baselines with a severity that grows with the mismatch.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Resampling target label proportions on existing benchmarks to create controlled mismatch will show alignment-based methods degrading below no-adaptation baselines beyond a modest mismatch level, while self-training degrades more gracefully.
why_important: Real deployments almost never have matched label proportions across domains, so a failure mode invisible on benchmarks is a failure mode guaranteed in practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The theoretical objection is known, but a quantitative mismatch-severity curve across popular methods on vision benchmarks, framed as a benchmark-design flaw, may be unoccupied territory.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one benchmark pair, resample target class proportions at several mismatch severities, run marginal-alignment and self-training methods at each severity, and plot adaptation gain versus mismatch.
main_risk: Resampling reduces target sample size at high mismatch, so accuracy changes must be disentangled from sample-size effects with matched-size controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Marginal alignment is treated as a safe default that at worst does nothing, and label-proportion mismatch is regarded as a corner case.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The harm is a mathematical consequence of forcing marginals to match under different mixing weights, so the only question is the severity threshold, not the existence of the effect.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One dataset pair, three target-prior resamplings, one adversarial-alignment method versus source-only, plot gain versus mismatch in a day.

one_line_idea: Given a foundation-model backbone, plain confidence-thresholded self-training beats every sophisticated alignment-based adaptation method across the standard benchmark suite.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Self-training with pseudo-labels is often reported as a component or baseline in adaptation pipelines, but the field's headline methods remain alignment- and discrepancy-based composites.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] With strong pretrained features, pseudo-label quality on target data crosses the threshold where self-training is self-reinforcing rather than error-amplifying, making it strictly dominant over alignment objectives that distort features.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A controlled bake-off on foundation backbones will show tuned-simple self-training at or above the best composite methods on most standard adaptation pairs, with the exceptions concentrated where zero-shot target accuracy is very low.
why_important: Establishing the correct simple baseline redirects the field toward the genuinely unsolved regime, which is adaptation when initial target accuracy is too low for self-training.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The claim is folk knowledge in some circles, but a rigorous bake-off with equalized tuning budgets across method families on modern backbones may not exist in published form.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a foundation backbone and a tuning budget, run self-training and three composite methods over the standard benchmark suite with identical budgets, and compare mean and per-pair results.
main_risk: Self-training has its own failure regime under severe initial error, and cherry-picking benchmark pairs where zero-shot accuracy is high would bias the bake-off in its favor.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Composite alignment methods are assumed to be ahead of self-training because they top published leaderboards.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Published leaderboards mostly compare against self-training implementations from the weak-backbone era, so the ordering may be an artifact of stale baselines.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three benchmark pairs, one backbone, tuned self-training versus one current composite method at equal budget, two days.

one_line_idea: Zero-shot vision-language models have effectively saturated office-style adaptation benchmarks, making continued method development on them uninformative.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Several classic adaptation benchmarks consist of everyday object categories across modest style gaps, a regime where zero-shot vision-language classification is now strong without any target data.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On these benchmarks, zero-shot performance of public vision-language models is within a small margin of the best published adaptation results that use unlabeled target data, implying the benchmarks no longer measure adaptation ability.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A direct comparison will show zero-shot classification matching or exceeding a majority of published adaptation numbers on the classic benchmark pairs, while genuinely hard pairs with fine-grained or low-level shifts remain unsaturated.
why_important: Fields calibrate progress by benchmarks; if the reference benchmarks are saturated by a method that ignores the problem setup, reported progress on them is measurement noise.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Zero-shot numbers on adaptation benchmarks have surely been computed piecemeal, but a saturation audit across the benchmark suite with explicit implications for benchmark retirement may not be assembled anywhere.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two or three public vision-language models zero-shot on the full set of classic adaptation pairs and tabulate against the recent published state of the art per pair.
main_risk: Class-name prompting choices affect zero-shot accuracy materially, so the audit must report sensitivity to prompt construction to be credible.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The classic benchmarks are still treated as live measurement instruments, since papers continue to report incremental gains on them.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The benchmarks were designed when models had never seen most visual styles, an assumption that web-scale pretraining has made false for everyday categories.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One public vision-language model, zero-shot on all pairs of one classic benchmark, compare to recent leaderboard numbers, a few hours.

one_line_idea: Unsupervised model selection, not adaptation method choice, is the dominant source of variance in domain adaptation outcomes, and reported method gains are smaller than selection-induced spread.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Domain adaptation lacks labeled target validation data, so checkpoint and hyperparameter selection must use proxies, yet papers typically report a single selected result per method without quantifying selection uncertainty.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The spread of target accuracy across defensible unsupervised selection criteria applied to one method's training run exceeds the typical published gap between competing methods, meaning the literature's method rankings are inside the selection noise band.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Applying several established unsupervised selection criteria to identical training runs of several methods will produce accuracy spreads per method that are larger than the median between-method gap reported on the same benchmarks.
why_important: If selection dominates method choice, the field's real open problem is unsupervised validation, and method-ranking papers are measuring the wrong variable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Selection criteria have been compared in isolation, but a variance decomposition pitting selection spread against method gaps as the headline quantity may be new framing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train several adaptation methods on several benchmark pairs, save dense checkpoints, apply a panel of unsupervised selection criteria, and decompose target-accuracy variance into method, pair, and selection components.
main_risk: The panel of selection criteria must be defensible and pre-registered, since including deliberately bad criteria would inflate the selection variance artificially.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Readers assume the selected checkpoints in papers reflect a solved or minor selection step rather than a major hidden degree of freedom.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Unsupervised proxies correlate weakly with target accuracy in the shifted regime by definition of the problem, so large selection spread is the expected default, not the exception.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, one pair, dense checkpoints, three selection criteria, measure accuracy spread versus a published method gap, one day.

one_line_idea: Source data hurts more than it helps once a strong foundation initialization exists: source-free adaptation matches or beats joint source-plus-target training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard adaptation assumes simultaneous access to labeled source and unlabeled target data, while source-free variants adapt a source-trained model without source data and are usually framed as a constrained, weaker setting.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] With a foundation-model initialization, continued training on source data anchors the model to source-specific decision structure, so removing source data during adaptation is neutral or beneficial rather than a handicap.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Matched-budget comparisons will show source-free pipelines equaling or exceeding joint training on a majority of benchmark pairs when both start from the same foundation initialization, reversing the presumed ordering of the two settings.
why_important: Source-free adaptation is also the privacy-compatible and logistics-friendly setting, so evidence that it costs nothing would change default practice and data-retention requirements.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Source-free methods exist in volume, but a clean causal comparison isolating the marginal value of source-data access at fixed initialization and budget may not have been made central anywhere.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several benchmark pairs, fine-tune the same foundation initialization with and without source data in the adaptation phase at matched compute, using the same target-side machinery, and compare target accuracy.
main_risk: The result may hinge on how much source knowledge is already in the fine-tuned starting checkpoint, so the starting-point definition must be varied to check robustness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Source access is assumed to be strictly valuable, with source-free treated as damage control for when data cannot be shared.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information source data provides, task definition and class structure, is already captured by the initialization, leaving mostly its domain-specific biases as the marginal contribution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two pairs, same initialization, adapt with and without source batches in the loss, matched steps, compare target accuracy in a day.

one_line_idea: A cheap a-priori adaptability score computed from foundation-model feature geometry predicts whether unsupervised adaptation will help, do nothing, or hurt on a given domain pair.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Practitioners cannot currently tell in advance whether running an adaptation method on a new domain pair will improve their model, and adaptation methods sometimes degrade performance.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Simple statistics of source and target embeddings under a frozen foundation model, such as class-cluster overlap and marginal distance decomposed into class-relevant and class-irrelevant directions, carry enough signal to predict the sign and rough magnitude of adaptation gain before any adaptation runs.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a broad grid of domain pairs and methods, a score fit on a subset of pairs will predict the sign of adaptation gain on held-out pairs well above chance, and its errors will concentrate on pairs with unusual label-shift structure.
why_important: A reliable go or no-go signal converts adaptation from a gamble into a decision procedure, which matters more for practice than another point of average accuracy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Transferability estimation exists for choosing source models, but pre-run prediction of unsupervised adaptation gain, as opposed to transfer accuracy, may be an unformalized problem.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble many domain pairs from existing benchmarks, run two adaptation methods on each to obtain ground-truth gains, compute candidate embedding statistics per pair, and evaluate held-out-pair prediction of gain sign and magnitude.
main_risk: The grid of available benchmark pairs is small and correlated, so the score could overfit benchmark idiosyncrasies and fail on genuinely new domain types.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Whether adaptation helps is treated as an empirical question answered by running the method, not something predictable from data statistics alone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptation gain is bounded by how much recoverable structure the target embedding already contains, and that quantity is directly measurable from the embeddings themselves.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten domain pairs, one method, three candidate statistics, check rank correlation between statistics and realized gains, two days.

one_line_idea: Domain invariance is the wrong objective: methods that succeed do so through implicit class-conditional alignment, and enforcing pure marginal invariance strictly removes target-discriminative information.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Domain-invariant representation learning is the stated objective of a large family of adaptation methods, yet invariance to domain provably conflicts with discriminability whenever domain and label are dependent.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Successful runs of invariance-based methods achieve their gains during phases where the learned representation is not actually domain-invariant but conditionally aligned given predicted class, so measured invariance will anti-correlate with target accuracy within training trajectories.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Instrumenting training runs with independent probes for domain predictability and target accuracy will show that checkpoints with the least domain information are not the checkpoints with the best target accuracy, and the correlation across checkpoints will be negative in the late phase.
why_important: If the field's stated objective anti-correlates with its goal, method design and theory are optimizing a misdirected quantity and should be reframed around conditional alignment.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The theoretical tension is documented, but trajectory-level empirical audits correlating achieved invariance with achieved transfer across popular methods may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train invariance-based methods on several pairs, checkpoint densely, measure domain-probe accuracy and target accuracy per checkpoint, and report their relationship within and across runs.
main_risk: Domain-probe capacity choices affect measured invariance, so probes must be standardized and reported at multiple capacities.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More domain invariance is assumed to mean better transfer, since invariance is the named goal of the method family.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Whenever class proportions differ across domains, some domain information is label information, and destroying it must destroy accuracy.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One adversarial-alignment run, dense checkpoints, domain probe versus target accuracy correlation, one day.

one_line_idea: In dense-prediction domain adaptation, a large share of reported gains comes from resolution, crop, and class-frequency handling rather than from distribution-alignment machinery.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Semantic-segmentation adaptation pipelines bundle alignment objectives with strong engineering choices such as multi-scale training, class-balanced sampling, and high-resolution cropping strategies, and ablations rarely isolate these factors across papers.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Applying only the input-pipeline and sampling engineering of leading segmentation-adaptation methods, with no adaptation objective at all, recovers a majority of their reported gain over naive source training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A decomposition study will show the engineering-only variant closing most of the gap between naive baselines and full methods on standard synthetic-to-real segmentation tasks, with the alignment objective contributing a modest residual.
why_important: Correct credit assignment determines what the community builds next; if pipelines rather than objectives drive gains, objective-design papers are optimizing the residual while presenting themselves as the main effect.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual ablations exist inside papers, but a cross-method decomposition run under one codebase with engineering and objective factors crossed may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reimplement two leading segmentation-adaptation methods in one codebase with switchable engineering and objective components, run the two-by-two factorial on a standard task, and attribute gains.
main_risk: Engineering and objectives may interact positively, so the factorial must be reported in full rather than as marginal effects only.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported gains are attributed to the named adaptation objectives, since those are the papers' contributions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense prediction is notoriously sensitive to scale and sampling choices, and these choices differ systematically between baseline and proposed configurations in the literature.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, engineering-only ablation on one synthetic-to-real task, compare to published full-method and baseline numbers, two days.

one_line_idea: Adaptation methods developed on synthetic-to-real style gaps systematically fail on real-to-real shifts such as geography and time, because the two gap types have different structure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A large fraction of adaptation research validates on synthetic-to-real transfers, whose gaps are dominated by rendering statistics, while deployment shifts are usually real-to-real changes in geography, time, sensor, or population.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Methods tuned for rendering-gap transfer exploit low-level regularities absent in real-to-real shifts, so their ranking and even their sign of benefit fail to transfer from the synthetic-to-real regime to real-to-real regimes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A cross-regime evaluation will show low rank correlation between method performance on synthetic-to-real tasks and on real-to-real tasks, with some celebrated methods providing no benefit in the latter regime.
why_important: If the field's main validation regime is unrepresentative, its accumulated method ranking is misleading for nearly all practical adopters.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Both regimes have benchmarks, but a deliberate regime-transfer study of the method stack, framed around the structural difference between rendering gaps and real-world gaps, may be unclaimed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select methods spanning alignment, self-training, and image-translation families, evaluate each on matched synthetic-to-real and real-to-real tasks, and compare per-regime rankings.
main_risk: Real-to-real tasks vary widely among themselves, so several distinct real-to-real shifts are needed before concluding regime-level generality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Strong synthetic-to-real results are read as evidence of general adaptation capability rather than regime-specific fit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rendering gaps concentrate in textures and low-level statistics that translation-style methods directly model, while geographic shifts change object frequencies and layouts, which those methods do not touch.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One translation-based method and one self-training method on one synthetic-to-real and one geographic-shift task, compare gain patterns, two days.

one_line_idea: With foundation-model backbones, the gap between domain-generalization algorithms and empirical risk minimization shrinks to zero, making algorithm-centric generalization research empirically unmotivated in the current regime.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Prior published evaluations under fair model selection reported that empirical risk minimization is competitive with most domain-generalization algorithms on standard multi-domain benchmarks, and backbones have strengthened substantially since those studies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Whatever residual advantage generalization algorithms had is a decreasing function of backbone quality, so on current foundation backbones the algorithm effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero while the backbone effect dominates by an order of magnitude.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-running a representative algorithm suite across several backbone generations under strict source-only model selection will show algorithm-attributable variance shrinking with backbone quality and losing statistical significance at the frontier.
why_important: The result would redirect effort from algorithm design to data and backbone questions, or alternatively sharpen exactly which shift regimes still reward algorithmic intervention.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The competitiveness of plain training is known; the backbone-quality scaling of the algorithm effect, treated as the primary object of study, may not be.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cross three backbone generations with a suite of generalization algorithms on standard multi-domain benchmarks under source-only selection, and estimate algorithm and backbone variance components with confidence intervals.
main_risk: Frontier backbones may have pretraining exposure to benchmark-like imagery, which would compress measured gaps for contamination reasons rather than the hypothesized reason.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Many researchers still treat algorithmic invariance machinery as the path to out-of-distribution generalization, with backbone choice as an implementation detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generalization algorithms mainly constrain how features are combined, and as pretrained features become sufficient statistics for the label, the room for such constraints to matter vanishes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two backbones spanning eras, plain training versus two generalization algorithms on one benchmark, compare gaps per backbone, two days.

one_line_idea: Domain-generalization benchmarks primarily rank pretrained backbones rather than generalization algorithms, and published algorithm rankings are noise around a backbone-determined score.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Reported results on multi-domain benchmarks conflate backbone choice, selection protocol, and algorithm, and papers frequently differ in the first two while claiming differences in the third.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A variance decomposition over the published literature and controlled reruns will attribute the large majority of score variance to backbone and selection protocol, with algorithm identity explaining a small residual that fails to replicate across reruns.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Controlled reruns with seeds and fixed protocols will show between-algorithm variance comparable to between-seed variance, while backbone substitution moves scores by many multiples of both.
why_important: If the benchmark instrument mostly measures the backbone, the field needs either new instruments or explicit reporting standards that prevent backbone effects from being sold as algorithmic progress.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Critiques of selection protocols exist, but a formal variance decomposition of the benchmark literature quantifying what the scores actually measure may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rerun a factorial of backbones, algorithms, and seeds on one benchmark under one protocol, fit a variance-components model, and compare component magnitudes.
main_risk: The factorial is compute-heavy, and pruning it risks unbalanced designs that bias the variance estimates.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark score differences between papers are read as evidence about algorithms, since that is what the papers claim to compare.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Feature quality upper-bounds transfer performance, and modern backbones differ enormously in feature quality while algorithms only reweight the same features.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, two backbones, three algorithms, three seeds, compare variance components, three days.

one_line_idea: Invariance-penalty methods fail on vision benchmarks because the annotated environments are not causally meaningful, and with environments constructed from capture metadata the same methods start working.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Invariance-penalty objectives assume environments that vary spuriously correlated factors while preserving causal structure, but vision benchmarks define environments by dataset provenance or style, which mixes many factors arbitrarily.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The reported failure of invariance penalties is an environment-quality failure rather than a theory failure, so re-partitioning existing data into environments aligned with plausible nuisance factors, such as capture hardware or acquisition context, will recover measurable invariance-penalty gains over plain training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Holding data fixed and swapping environment definitions from provenance-based to metadata-based will change invariance-method performance from at-or-below plain training to consistently above it on shifts aligned with the chosen nuisance factor.
why_important: The community may have discarded a correct principle because its benchmarks tested it with malformed inputs, which would be a costly false negative for the field.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Environment-quality has been discussed theoretically, but a controlled same-data environment-swap experiment on vision benchmarks may not have been executed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick datasets with rich capture metadata, define provenance-based and metadata-based environment partitions of identical data, train invariance methods under both, and evaluate on shifts targeting the metadata factor.
main_risk: Metadata-based environments may correlate with labels, which would confound the comparison and require careful stratification.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Invariance penalties are widely considered empirically refuted for realistic vision tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The refutation experiments never satisfied the methods' stated assumptions, so the empirical record tests the benchmarks as much as the methods.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One metadata-rich dataset, two environment partitions, one invariance method versus plain training, evaluate on a metadata-aligned shift, two days.

one_line_idea: Weight-averaging and flat-minima methods improve domain-generalization scores through generic variance reduction that helps in-distribution equally, not through any shift-specific mechanism.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Weight-averaging approaches are among the strongest reported methods on multi-domain benchmarks, and their benefit is attributed to flat minima improving out-of-distribution generalization.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The improvement is a uniform accuracy lift from implicit ensembling that applies identically to in-distribution test data, so the ratio of out-of-distribution to in-distribution gain will be near one, contradicting shift-specific explanations.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring both in-distribution and out-of-distribution gains of weight averaging across benchmarks will show proportional lifts, and effective-robustness-style analysis will place averaged models on the same trend line as their non-averaged counterparts.
why_important: Mechanistic misattribution steers follow-up research; if averaging is generic variance reduction, it belongs in every baseline rather than being counted as generalization progress.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Weight averaging is well studied, but the specific test distinguishing uniform lift from shift-specific lift on generalization benchmarks may not be settled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with and without weight averaging on multi-domain benchmarks, measure held-in-domain and held-out-domain accuracy for both, and compare the gain ratio to one across settings.
main_risk: Held-in-domain test splits on these benchmarks are small, making the in-distribution gain estimate noisy.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Flat minima are believed to confer specifically out-of-distribution benefits, which is why averaging is framed as a generalization method.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ensembling lifts accuracy roughly uniformly across test distributions in most reported settings, and weight averaging approximates ensembling.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, one backbone, averaging on versus off, record both in-domain and out-domain gains, one day.

one_line_idea: A leakage audit of the domain-generalization literature: quantifying how much of reported progress evaporates under strictly source-only model selection.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Model selection using held-out target-domain data leaks test information, the issue is documented, yet selection protocols in published papers remain heterogeneous and are often under-specified.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial fraction of claimed post-baseline progress on multi-domain benchmarks is attributable to lenient selection protocols, and re-selecting under a strict source-only rule will compress the published progress curve toward flatness.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Reproducing a sample of published configurations and re-running model selection under a strict protocol will reduce the median claimed improvement over plain training by a large fraction and flip the sign for some methods.
why_important: The audit converts a known qualitative concern into a quantitative correction factor for the literature, informing how much trust downstream users should place in leaderboard progress.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The protocol critique is established; an executed quantitative audit across many published methods with a single strict re-selection may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select a representative sample of published methods with public code, re-run each under the strict source-only selection protocol on the same benchmarks, and report published-versus-audited gaps.
main_risk: Reproduction failures unrelated to selection could be misattributed to leakage, so each reproduction must first match the published number under the original protocol.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Readers assume reported gains would survive honest selection because the leakage issue is considered common knowledge that authors avoid.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Selection under shift is close to the core difficulty of the problem, so leniency there can manufacture nearly arbitrary apparent gains.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two published methods with code, re-select strictly on one benchmark, compare against published numbers, two days.

one_line_idea: Pretraining data diversity, not model scale, is the dominant controllable factor for out-of-domain generalization at fixed compute.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Out-of-distribution performance of foundation models improves with scale, but scale simultaneously increases parameters, data quantity, and data diversity, and these are rarely disentangled.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At fixed compute and fixed data quantity, increasing the diversity of pretraining data sources yields larger out-of-domain gains than increasing model size, and diversity effects dominate the out-of-domain scaling curve.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A controlled grid over model size and source diversity at matched compute will show out-of-domain accuracy responding more steeply to the diversity axis, while in-distribution accuracy responds comparably to both axes.
why_important: The result would give a concrete lever for building robust models cheaply and would reframe robustness as a data curation problem rather than a scale problem.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-centric robustness findings exist for specific model families, but a compute-matched factorial isolating diversity from quantity and size at trainable scales may be open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain small models on datasets constructed at fixed size but varying source diversity, across two or three model sizes, then evaluate a battery of shifted downstream tasks and fit response surfaces.
main_risk: Diversity is hard to define operationally, and results may depend on the chosen diversity metric more than on the underlying phenomenon.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scale is treated as the primary robustness driver, with the folk prescription being to train bigger on more data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Robustness to a shift plausibly requires pretraining coverage near that shift, and coverage is a function of diversity rather than of parameter count.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two small pretraining runs at equal token and compute budget, single-source versus multi-source data, compare downstream shifted-task accuracy, several days of small-scale training.

one_line_idea: Gains from style-based augmentation on stylized benchmarks anti-correlate with performance on real geographic and temporal shifts, revealing style benchmarks as a misleading target.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Style and texture augmentation methods report strong results on benchmarks whose domains are artistic or rendering styles, and such benchmarks are widely used to certify generalization ability.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Optimizing invariance to style consumes model capacity and distorts features that matter for real-world shifts, so style-benchmark gains predict zero or negative gains on geographic and temporal shift tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a set of augmentation and stylization methods, the correlation between stylized-benchmark improvement and real-shift improvement will be near zero or negative, with capacity-heavy stylization showing the largest divergence.
why_important: If certifying on style benchmarks selects methods that fail on deployment-relevant shifts, the community's benchmark habit actively misdirects method development.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Concerns about stylized benchmarks are voiced informally, but a quantitative cross-benchmark correlation study of style-oriented methods against real-shift outcomes may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a set of models with varying style-augmentation strength, evaluate each on stylized benchmarks and on real geographic and temporal shift sets, and estimate the cross-benchmark gain correlation.
main_risk: Real-shift datasets embed label-distribution changes that could mask a genuine positive correlation, so label-shift correction should be applied before correlating.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Style-benchmark improvements are read as evidence of general robustness because style gaps are visually dramatic.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Real shifts mostly change content statistics, object frequency, and context rather than rendering style, so style invariance targets the wrong factor.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three augmentation strengths, one backbone, evaluate on one stylized benchmark and one geographic-shift set, check the gain relationship, two days.

one_line_idea: Per unit of in-distribution accuracy, frozen-feature linear probes generalize across domains better than end-to-end fine-tuned models, and the gap widens with shift severity.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Prior work has reported that fine-tuning can distort pretrained features and reduce out-of-distribution performance relative to linear probing in some regimes, but common practice still defaults to full fine-tuning for downstream deployment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The probing-versus-fine-tuning robustness tradeoff is systematic and monotone in shift severity, so an accuracy-matched comparison across many shift levels will show probes dominating fine-tuned models out-of-distribution at every matched in-distribution accuracy level.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructing accuracy-matched pairs of probed and fine-tuned models and evaluating across graded shift severities will show a robustness gap favoring probes that grows with severity, holding across several foundation backbones.
why_important: A clean severity-resolved law would give practitioners a principled rule for when to freeze features, replacing folklore with a measurable tradeoff curve.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The phenomenon is documented at specific operating points; its systematic severity-resolved, accuracy-matched characterization across modern backbones may be open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For each backbone, train probes and fine-tuned variants to matched in-distribution accuracy by early stopping, evaluate on a graded shift battery, and plot the robustness gap versus severity.
main_risk: Matching in-distribution accuracy exactly is fiddly, and mismatches would confound the comparison since robustness correlates with accuracy.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Full fine-tuning is assumed superior overall, with any robustness loss considered minor relative to its in-distribution gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning reshapes features toward source-specific directions by construction, and the harm of that reshaping should scale with how far the test distribution moves.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, probe versus early-stopped fine-tune at matched source accuracy, evaluate on three shift severities, one day.

one_line_idea: Compositional shift, where familiar attributes and objects appear in novel combinations, is a distinct failure axis of vision foundation models that standard domain-generalization metrics never measure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Domain-generalization evaluation focuses on style, corruption, and provenance shifts, while real deployments also encounter novel combinations of individually familiar factors, such as known objects in unusual contexts or configurations.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation models degrade sharply and systematically on held-out combinations even when every constituent factor is well represented in training, and this degradation is uncorrelated with their scores on standard shift benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A benchmark constructed by holding out attribute-object or object-context combinations will show large accuracy drops across models, and model rankings on it will correlate poorly with rankings on style and corruption benchmarks.
why_important: If compositional shift is an independent axis, current robustness certifications say nothing about it, and deployments face an unmeasured failure class.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Compositional generalization is studied in other contexts, but its formulation as a distribution-shift axis with severity control and cross-benchmark correlation analysis for vision foundation models may be open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build combination-held-out splits from richly annotated existing datasets, evaluate a panel of foundation models zero-shot and probed, and compare drop patterns with the same models' standard shift scores.
main_risk: Constructing genuinely held-out combinations is difficult given opaque web-scale pretraining data, so degradation could be underestimated by hidden exposure.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Strong performance on standard shift suites is taken to imply broad out-of-distribution competence, implicitly covering compositional novelty.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Statistical learning binds features to their co-occurrence statistics, and no amount of per-factor coverage guarantees behavior on unseen joint configurations.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Use an attribute-annotated dataset, hold out one attribute-object cell, test zero-shot accuracy on the held-out cell versus seen cells, hours.

one_line_idea: Leave-one-domain-out evaluation has such high variance across the choice of held-out domain that most published domain-generalization comparisons are statistically undecidable.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard multi-domain benchmarks contain only a handful of domains, and the convention averages over each-domain-held-out runs, treating the domains as exchangeable and the average as a stable quantity.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The distribution over held-out-domain results is so heavy-tailed and method-domain interaction so strong that the averaged score has confidence intervals wider than typical reported method gaps, rendering most pairwise method comparisons undecidable at benchmark scale.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A resampling analysis over domains and seeds will show that the sign of the difference between many published method pairs flips depending on which domains are included, and that stabilizing rankings would require several times more domains than any current benchmark has.
why_important: The analysis quantifies how many domains an informative benchmark needs, converting benchmark design from convention to statistics.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Seed variance is sometimes reported, but domain-sampling variance as the dominant uncertainty term, with sample-size requirements derived from it, may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rerun a set of methods across all held-out-domain configurations with multiple seeds, bootstrap over domains, and report the fraction of method pairs whose ordering is stable.
main_risk: With few domains available, the bootstrap itself is noisy, so conclusions should be framed as lower bounds on the instability.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Averages over three to six held-out domains are treated as adequate summaries of generalization capability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Domains are the unit of inference in this problem, and no other field would accept population claims from a sample of four units.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, three methods, all held-out configurations, bootstrap the method ordering over domains, compute stability, two days.

one_line_idea: Textual descriptions of a target domain, used to steer a vision-language model, recover a large fraction of the benefit that unsupervised adaptation obtains from actual target images.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-language models accept natural-language conditioning, and target-domain knowledge is often available as a verbal description, such as nighttime infrared footage from a highway camera, before any target images are collected.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial part of the information adaptation methods extract from unlabeled target images is coarse domain identity, which language can supply directly, so prompt-level domain conditioning will close a meaningful fraction of the source-to-target gap without any target data.
