falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across several shift tasks, domain-conditioned prompting will close a consistent nontrivial fraction of the gap that image-based unsupervised adaptation closes, and the two will be partially redundant when combined.
why_important: Zero-data adaptation via language would help exactly the deployments that cannot collect target data in advance, and would quantify how much of adaptation is coarse domain identification.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt engineering for robustness exists piecemeal, but a controlled equivalence study measuring language-conditioning gain against image-based adaptation gain on shared tasks may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For each shift task, compare zero-shot, domain-described prompting, image-based adaptation, and their combination, reporting gap-closure fractions on the same backbone.
main_risk: Prompt sensitivity is high, so description construction must be systematized, ideally generated by a fixed procedure rather than hand-tuned per task.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adaptation is assumed to require samples from the target distribution, with language regarded as insufficient to convey distributional information.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The text tower embeds rich priors about visual domains from pretraining, and a short description may index those priors as effectively as a batch of images does.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One shift task, five systematic domain-description prompts versus one adaptation method, compare gap closure, hours.

one_line_idea: Latent domain discovery from foundation-model features produces better environment partitions for invariance-based training than human-annotated domain labels.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Invariance-based methods consume environment labels, which benchmarks supply from dataset provenance, yet provenance may not track the factors that actually vary spuriously with labels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Clustering training data in frozen foundation-model feature space, after projecting out label-predictive directions, yields environment partitions that better isolate spurious factors, so invariance methods trained on discovered environments outperform the same methods trained on annotated domains.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On benchmarks with known spurious factors, discovered-environment training will beat annotated-environment training for the same invariance method, and the discovered partitions will measurably align with the spurious factor more than provenance does.
why_important: If environments can be discovered better than they are annotated, invariance methods become applicable to the vast majority of datasets that lack any domain annotation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Environment inference has been explored in restricted settings; using foundation-feature geometry with label-direction removal as the discovery mechanism at benchmark scale may be untried.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On datasets with a known spurious attribute, run the discovery pipeline, train one invariance method with annotated versus discovered environments, and evaluate on splits where the spurious correlation is reversed.
main_risk: Discovered clusters may capture label information despite the projection step, which would convert the invariance penalty into an accuracy penalty.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Human domain annotation is treated as the gold standard input to invariance methods, with discovery seen as a fallback.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Provenance is an administrative fact about data collection, while spurious variation is a statistical fact about features, and there is no reason the two should coincide.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One spurious-correlation dataset, cluster features into environments, train one invariance method both ways, compare reversed-split accuracy, one day.

one_line_idea: Frozen foundation-model embeddings with classical two-sample tests detect deployment distribution shift better than dedicated learned shift detectors.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Production monitoring needs to detect when input distributions change, and the dedicated literature offers learned detectors, density models, and per-task calibration, all of which add training and maintenance burden.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The detection problem becomes easy in a good representation, so a frozen general-purpose embedding combined with classical multivariate two-sample statistics matches or beats specialized detectors across realistic shift types at a fraction of the operational cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a battery of natural and synthetic shifts at varying severities and sample sizes, the embedding-plus-classical-test approach will dominate specialized methods in detection power at matched false-positive rates for most shift types.
why_important: Monitoring is deployed far more widely than adaptation, and a simple dominant recipe would set the correct default for industry practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pieces of this recipe are used ad hoc; a rigorous power-versus-sample-size comparison across shift families against the dedicated-method literature may be unassembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix shift scenarios with controlled severity, run the simple recipe and several dedicated detectors, and report power curves versus sample size at fixed false-positive rate.
main_risk: Power depends on which embedding is used, and a single embedding choice may not represent the recipe fairly across shift types.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Shift detection is presented as requiring task-specific learned components, which is why dedicated methods keep being developed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Two-sample testing in a representation that linearizes semantic variation is close to the statistically optimal reduction of the problem, leaving little room for specialized machinery.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One embedding, one kernel-based two-sample test versus one learned detector on three shift types, power at fixed sample size, one day.

one_line_idea: Most distribution shifts flagged by monitoring systems do not harm accuracy, and harm-calibrated detection, not shift detection, is the correct monitoring objective.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Statistical tests detect any distributional difference given enough samples, including benign changes such as compression settings or camera upgrades that leave model accuracy unchanged, and every alarm consumes engineering attention.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In realistic deployment streams the majority of statistically detectable shifts are accuracy-neutral, so detectors optimized for distributional sensitivity have precision far below what harm-targeted detectors achieve at equal recall of genuinely harmful shifts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Instrumenting shift scenarios with ground-truth accuracy change will show weak correlation between statistical shift magnitude and realized harm, and a detector trained or calibrated on harm proxies will strictly dominate the precision-recall tradeoff of pure distributional detectors.
why_important: Alarm fatigue is the reported failure mode of monitoring in practice, and reframing the objective from shift to harm addresses the actual operational problem.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The shift-versus-harm distinction is acknowledged in scattered places, but benchmark construction and detector evaluation centered on harm labels rather than shift labels may be largely unoccupied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build scenarios pairing each shift with measured accuracy change on labeled probes, evaluate distributional detectors and harm-proxy detectors on harmful-shift recall versus false-alarm rate, and compare curves.
main_risk: Harm ground truth requires labels under shift, which is expensive, so scenario coverage may be narrow and favor certain shift families.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detecting distribution change is treated as inherently valuable, with harm assessment deferred to human follow-up.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Statistical detectability scales with sample size without bound while harm does not, so the two objectives provably diverge as monitoring windows grow.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Five shifts with known accuracy impact, one two-sample detector, check ordering of alarm strength versus realized harm, hours.

one_line_idea: Unlabeled accuracy-estimation methods fail precisely on the shift types where monitoring needs them most, and a failure taxonomy predicts when their estimates can be trusted.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Methods that estimate a model's accuracy on unlabeled shifted data from confidence or agreement statistics are increasingly proposed for deployment monitoring, and their published validations concentrate on covariate-style shifts.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] These estimators share an assumption that confidence remains informative of correctness under the shift, which holds for low-level covariate shifts but fails under semantic, label-prior, and spurious-correlation shifts, producing confidently wrong accuracy estimates exactly when the model is most degraded.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A stratified evaluation across shift families will show estimation error concentrated in semantic and correlation shifts, with errors systematically optimistic there, and near-perfect estimates only on the covariate shifts the methods were validated on.
why_important: An accuracy estimator that is optimistic during dangerous shifts is worse than no estimator, since it certifies broken models as healthy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual failure reports exist; a systematic shift-family taxonomy of estimator validity with a practical trust rule may not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble shifts spanning corruption, prior change, semantic novelty, and correlation reversal with labeled ground truth, run several estimators, and map signed estimation error by family.
main_risk: Estimator hyperparameters tuned per shift could mask the failure pattern, so tuning must be frozen before the stratified evaluation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Positive results on corruption suites are read as evidence these estimators are ready for general deployment monitoring.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The estimators consume the model's own confidence, and shifts that break the model also break its confidence signal, making the failure correlated with the harm.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One estimator, one corruption shift versus one correlation-reversal shift with labels, compare signed estimation errors, hours.

one_line_idea: The accuracy-on-the-line phenomenon is a property of shared pretraining lineages, and it breaks for adapted, fine-tuned, or intervention-modified models, undermining its use for monitoring.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Prior work reported strong linear relationships between in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy across model collections, and such trends are increasingly used to predict shifted performance without labels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The linear trend is generated by models sharing pretraining data and training recipes, so models modified by test-time adaptation, robust fine-tuning, or targeted interventions will fall systematically off the line, making line-based prediction unreliable exactly for the models robustness research produces.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Plotting in-distribution versus out-of-distribution accuracy for a collection including adapted and intervention-modified models will show significantly larger residuals for modified models than for vanilla ones, with residual sign depending on intervention type.
why_important: If the models most likely to be deployed after robustness work are the ones the line cannot predict, monitoring pipelines built on the line will mis-estimate exactly the deployed population.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Off-line outliers have been noted for specific robust models; a systematic study of which model-modification classes break the line, framed as a monitoring reliability question, may be open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble vanilla, fine-tuned, adapted, and intervention-modified variants across backbones, evaluate on paired in-distribution and shifted sets, and compare residual distributions to the vanilla-only fit.
main_risk: Line fits depend on axis transformations, and conclusions about residuals must be shown robust to the transformation choice.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The linear trend is treated as a near-law of nature that holds broadly enough to build label-free performance prediction on.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A regularity produced by a shared training distribution has no reason to constrain models whose training was deliberately pushed away from that shared distribution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten vanilla models plus five robust-fine-tuned variants on one in-distribution and one shifted set, compare residuals, one day.

one_line_idea: Embedding-space shift detection is dominated by low-level image statistics, masking semantic shifts; band-separated tests are needed to see what actually changed.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Shift detectors operating on deep embeddings report a single shift score, while real changes decompose into low-level factors like compression and color and high-level factors like content and population, with very different operational implications.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Standard embedding statistics respond much more strongly to low-level factors than to semantic factors of equal harm, so a semantic shift co-occurring with a mild low-level change is detected as the low-level change and its semantic component goes unnoticed.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In factorial scenarios crossing low-level and semantic changes, single-score detectors will show scores dominated by the low-level factor, while a decomposition that separates frequency-band and semantic-subspace components will recover both factors independently.
why_important: Monitoring that reports a shift but misattributes its nature triggers wrong responses, such as recalibrating a camera when the population changed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Shift attribution into interpretable low-level versus semantic components, validated on factorial scenarios, may be missing from the monitoring literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a factorial grid of low-level transformations crossed with semantic composition changes, run standard detectors and the band-separated variant, and measure factor-recovery accuracy.
main_risk: The semantic subspace must be defined without circularity, for example from an independent model, or the decomposition validates itself.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A large embedding-shift score is read as indicating meaningful change, with the nature of the change left to manual investigation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-level statistics permeate every dimension of learned embeddings, while semantic differences concentrate in lower-dimensional structure, so magnitude-based scores are biased toward the former.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One dataset, apply compression change versus class-mixture change calibrated to equal accuracy harm, compare a standard detector's scores, hours.

one_line_idea: Anytime-valid sequential tests on foundation-model embeddings give deployment shift alarms with controlled false-alarm rates, which matters more in practice than the detection-power race.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Deployment monitoring is sequential, with decisions made continuously as data arrives, yet most shift-detection research evaluates fixed-sample tests that do not control error under continuous monitoring.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Martingale-based and conformal sequential tests over frozen embeddings provide practically sufficient detection latency while guaranteeing false-alarm control under continuous monitoring, and the lack of such control, not lack of power, is why practitioners distrust current detectors.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On simulated month-long streams with rare injected shifts, fixed-sample detectors re-applied repeatedly will produce false-alarm rates far above nominal, while sequential-valid methods will hold their guarantees with detection latency within a small factor of the fixed-sample optimum.
why_important: A monitoring alarm that fires spuriously every week gets ignored, so error control under continuous operation is the binding constraint for adoption.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Sequential testing theory is mature, but its combination with foundation-model embeddings and an evaluation centered on operational false-alarm budgets for vision deployment may be unassembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate long streams from existing datasets with controlled shift injections, run repeated fixed-sample tests versus sequential-valid tests, and report realized false-alarm rates and detection latencies.
main_risk: Sequential methods can be conservative, and excessive latency on subtle harmful shifts would undercut the practical argument.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The field's implicit objective is maximal detection power on fixed samples, with repeated-testing error treated as an implementation footnote.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Repeated testing without correction inflates false alarms mechanically, so any deployment using fixed-sample tests continuously is operating far from its nominal error rate.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One simulated stream without any shift, repeated fixed-sample testing versus one conformal martingale, count false alarms over the stream, hours.

one_line_idea: Predicting per-sample correctness under shift is more tractable than predicting aggregate accuracy, and selective prediction transfers across shifts better than accuracy estimation does.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Label-free performance prediction under shift is usually framed as estimating a single aggregate accuracy number, which collapses heterogeneous per-sample behavior into one statistic and is known to fail under several shift types.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The per-sample question, whether this prediction is trustworthy, retains usable signal under shifts that break aggregate estimation, because instance-level features of failure generalize while population-level confidence calibration does not.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training a correctness predictor on one shift family and testing on others will retain most of its ranking quality for selective prediction, while aggregate accuracy estimators transferred the same way will show large systematic errors.
why_important: Deployments act per sample, deferring or escalating individual cases, so instance-level trust signals are directly actionable in a way aggregate estimates are not.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Selective prediction and accuracy estimation are studied separately; a direct cross-shift transferability comparison between the two problem framings may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On shifts with labels, train correctness predictors and accuracy estimators on a source shift family, evaluate ranking quality and estimation error respectively on held-out families, and compare degradation.
main_risk: Comparing a ranking metric with an estimation metric requires care to avoid apples-to-oranges conclusions, so both should be reduced to decision-level utility.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Aggregate accuracy estimation is treated as the canonical unlabeled-evaluation problem, with per-sample trust as a downstream application.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Aggregate estimation must implicitly solve calibration under shift, a strictly harder problem than preserving within-set correctness ranking.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One correctness predictor and one accuracy estimator trained on corruption shifts, both evaluated on one natural shift, compare usefulness, one day.

one_line_idea: Rankings from out-of-distribution detection benchmarks do not predict which methods detect harmful natural shift in deployment-like monitoring, revealing a benchmark-objective mismatch.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Out-of-distribution detection methods are ranked on suites that separate a training distribution from disjoint outlier datasets, and these rankings guide method choice for deployment monitoring where the actual task is flagging harmful drift.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The suite task, distinguishing wholly different datasets, rewards features irrelevant to detecting gradual harmful drift within a deployment distribution, so method rankings on the suites will correlate poorly with rankings on realistic drift-monitoring tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating a spectrum of detection methods on both standard outlier suites and constructed drift-monitoring scenarios will yield low rank correlation between the two orderings, with some suite leaders performing near chance on drift.
why_important: Practitioners select monitoring tools from suite leaderboards, and a demonstrated mismatch means those selections are effectively random for the deployment task.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Critiques of outlier suites exist, but a quantitative cross-task ranking-transfer study to drift monitoring may not have been executed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a broad method panel, evaluate on standard outlier suites and on drift scenarios built from temporally or geographically sliced real datasets, and compute cross-task rank correlation.
main_risk: Drift-scenario construction has many degrees of freedom, and an unrepresentative scenario set could understate the correlation unfairly.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Out-of-distribution detection benchmarks are treated as the appropriate certification for deployment monitoring capability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The suites test discrimination between datasets that differ in every statistic at once, providing no evidence about sensitivity to subtle within-pipeline change.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three detection methods, one outlier suite, one temporal-drift scenario, compare orderings, one day.

one_line_idea: Label-shift estimators silently return confident nonsense when class-conditional distributions also shift, and a cheap self-diagnostic can flag when their assumption is violated.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Classical label-shift estimation infers test class priors from unlabeled data under the assumption that class-conditional input distributions are unchanged, and this assumption is uncheckable directly without target labels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Realistic shifts almost always violate the conditional-invariance assumption to some degree, causing prior estimates with large errors that carry no warning sign, but internal consistency statistics of the estimator, such as confusion-matrix compatibility across data splits, can detect the violation without labels.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On shifts with controlled conditional change, prior-estimation error will grow smoothly with conditional-shift strength while the estimator reports nothing unusual, and the proposed consistency diagnostic will correlate strongly with the unobserved estimation error.
why_important: Prior correction is one of the few adaptation tools with clean theory, and a validity light would make it safely deployable instead of a hidden risk.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Robust variants of label-shift estimation exist, but a practical label-free diagnostic of assumption violation, validated against controlled conditional shifts in vision, may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct test sets crossing prior change with graded conditional change, run standard estimators, record estimation error, compute candidate diagnostics, and evaluate their correlation with error.
main_risk: The diagnostic could itself depend on the shift type, flagging some conditional changes while missing others, so shift-family coverage is essential.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Label-shift correction is regarded as a safe standard tool whose assumptions hold approximately in practice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nothing in a deployment guarantees conditional invariance, and estimators built on an unverifiable assumption fail without any observable symptom by construction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One dataset, prior change plus increasing input corruption on one class, watch prior-estimate error grow silently, hours.

one_line_idea: Drift root-cause attribution, assigning a detected shift to interpretable factors via counterfactual reweighting in foundation-feature space, is more valuable and more tractable than drift detection itself.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] When monitoring flags a shift, engineers must manually determine what changed, whether capture conditions, content mixture, or population, and this diagnosis step has no standard tooling despite being where the operational cost lies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Reweighting reference data to match the shifted stream within interpretable factor subspaces of a foundation embedding, and measuring how much each factor's reweighting explains the detected divergence, produces attribution that agrees with ground-truth causes in controlled scenarios.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On scenarios with known injected causes, the attribution procedure will rank the true factor first in a large majority of cases, including mixed-cause scenarios where it will approximately recover the mixing proportions.
why_important: Attribution turns an alarm into an action, and automated diagnosis would remove the main human bottleneck in monitoring pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Shift explanation appears in tabular settings; a factor-attribution framework over vision foundation features with counterfactual reweighting validation may be open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define factor subspaces for capture, content, and population using metadata or probe directions, inject single- and mixed-cause shifts into streams, and score the attribution against ground truth.
main_risk: Factor subspaces overlap in learned embeddings, and entangled factors may make clean attribution impossible beyond coarse categories.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detection is treated as the scientific problem and diagnosis as an engineering afterthought left to manual inspection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information needed for attribution is already present in which embedding directions moved, so the problem is representation and bookkeeping rather than new statistics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inject a pure capture-condition shift, check whether reweighting only the capture subspace explains most of the divergence, hours.

one_line_idea: Hidden batch effects inside single-domain vision test sets shrink effective sample size so much that standard error bars in evaluation papers are systematically overconfident.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test images within a dataset share cameras, photographers, sessions, and source websites, creating within-cluster correlation, yet reported confidence intervals treat test samples as independent draws.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cluster structure in standard test sets reduces effective sample size by a large factor for typical accuracy comparisons, so many published significant differences between models would not survive cluster-aware inference.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Recovering or estimating cluster structure in popular test sets and recomputing uncertainty with cluster-robust methods will widen confidence intervals substantially and render a nontrivial fraction of published model comparisons statistically undecided.
why_important: The community's inferential machinery assumes independence that data collection violates, which quietly corrupts every significance claim built on it.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Cluster-robust inference is standard in econometrics, but its application to vision benchmark test sets with estimated cluster structure may be absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate clusters in test sets via metadata where available and embedding similarity otherwise, recompute model-comparison uncertainty with cluster bootstrap, and compare interval widths against the i.i.d. analysis.
main_risk: Cluster estimation from embeddings could overstate correlation by grouping semantically similar but independently captured images.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Test-set size in the tens of thousands is assumed to make sampling error negligible for model comparison.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Correlated errors within shared-source clusters are exactly the structure that makes nominal sample size misleading, and web-collected datasets are built from such clusters.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One test set with source metadata, cluster bootstrap versus i.i.d. bootstrap on one model-pair comparison, compare interval widths, hours.

one_line_idea: Data augmentation is an unacknowledged train-time distribution shift, and its interaction with test-time shift explains part of why augmentation-trained models respond unpredictably to deployment drift.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Training pipelines apply aggressive augmentations that make the effective training distribution deliberately different from both the raw dataset and any deployment distribution, yet robustness analysis treats the raw dataset as the reference distribution.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The augmentation policy defines a reference envelope, and a model's response to a test-time shift depends primarily on whether the shift lies inside or outside that envelope, making the augmentation policy, not the raw data, the correct object for predicting shift response.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Characterizing shifts by their coverage under the training augmentation distribution will predict degradation better than distance from the raw data distribution, across models trained with different augmentation policies.
why_important: Practitioners reason about robustness relative to their dataset, while the actual determinant may be a policy choice buried in the training script, changing how robustness should be predicted and reported.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Augmentation-robustness links are known for specific corruptions; recasting the augmentation policy as the reference distribution for general shift-response prediction may be new framing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train models under several augmentation policies, define coverage scores of test shifts under each policy, and compare coverage against raw-data distance as predictors of per-shift degradation.
main_risk: Coverage under an augmentation distribution is nontrivial to estimate, and a crude estimator could fail for reasons unrelated to the hypothesis.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Augmentation is viewed as a generic regularizer, and robustness is discussed relative to the dataset rather than the augmented distribution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A model never sees the raw distribution during training, so any theory of its behavior anchored to the raw distribution is anchored to something the model has no direct relationship with.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two models differing only in augmentation policy, evaluate on shifts inside one policy's envelope and outside both, compare degradation patterns, one day.

one_line_idea: Dataset curation filters make benchmark test sets systematically easier than deployment data, and the curation-induced optimism is quantifiable by reconstructing the rejected data.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark datasets are assembled with quality filters, deduplication, canonical viewpoints, and annotator-agreement requirements, all of which remove exactly the ambiguous and atypical inputs that deployments must handle.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The accuracy gap between curated test sets and uncurated streams from the same nominal distribution is large, model-dependent, and dominated by the curation filters themselves, so re-collecting data with filters removed provides a direct measurement of curation optimism.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating models on filter-relaxed re-collections matched for content category will show accuracy drops substantially larger than test-set resampling noise, with model rankings partially reordered relative to the curated sets.
why_important: Curation optimism inflates every deployment forecast made from benchmark numbers, and quantifying it per filter tells us which curation choice does the damage.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Harder re-collections of specific benchmarks exist, but factor-attributed measurement of which curation filters cause how much optimism may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-collect data for a subset of classes with each curation filter selectively disabled, evaluate a model panel per condition, and attribute the accuracy gap across filters.
main_risk: Re-collection changes more than the intended filter, and time drift between original and new collection could confound the attribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Curated test accuracy is treated as an unbiased estimate of performance on the underlying visual task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Selection on quality and agreement is selection on easiness, and conditioning a test distribution on easiness biases accuracy upward by construction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For ten classes, scrape fresh unfiltered images, evaluate one model against its curated-set accuracy on the same classes, one day.

one_line_idea: Deployed vision models reshape the future data they receive, and this feedback loop breaks i.i.d. evaluation in a way measurable only through simulation-based protocols.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision systems in moderation, search ranking, autonomous capture, and camera-assist settings influence which images are subsequently created, retained, or submitted, making future inputs causally dependent on current model behavior.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under realistic feedback dynamics, model performance trajectories diverge substantially from what any static test set predicts, with error concentrating in regions the model's own decisions made rare in its observable stream, and simulation of the loop is sufficient to expose the divergence.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Closed-loop simulations where a model filters or ranks content that then conditions the next data batch will show static-test accuracy remaining stable while realized decision quality degrades measurably over rounds, for several plausible feedback mechanisms.
why_important: If evaluation cannot see feedback-induced degradation, systems can rot in deployment while dashboards report health, which is a governance problem as much as a technical one.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Performative prediction is studied theoretically and in recommendation settings; concrete closed-loop evaluation protocols for vision deployments may be largely absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a simulator where a model's filtering decisions determine the composition of subsequent batches drawn from a large image pool, run several feedback mechanisms, and track realized versus static-test performance over rounds.
main_risk: Simulated feedback mechanisms may not resemble real deployment dynamics, limiting external validity of any observed divergence.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Vision evaluation implicitly assumes the world generates images independently of the model, so feedback is ignored outside recommendation contexts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Any system whose outputs affect image creation or retention violates the independence assumption by definition, and most deployed vision systems have such pathways.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Simple simulation with a classifier filtering a stream that then oversamples accepted-like content, track accuracy drift over twenty rounds, hours.

one_line_idea: Shuffling time-stamped datasets hides temporal drift; time-respecting splits materially change both absolute accuracy and model rankings on the same data.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many vision datasets are collected over months or years and carry timestamps, but standard practice shuffles all data before splitting, destroying temporal structure and hiding any drift between collection and deployment eras.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training on early data and testing on late data from the same dataset will reveal consistent accuracy drops and ranking changes relative to shuffled splits, demonstrating that conventional splits overstate deployment performance even with zero nominal domain change.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across several timestamped datasets, time-respecting splits will show accuracy below shuffled splits by margins exceeding resampling noise, with the gap growing as the temporal distance between train and test windows increases.
why_important: Every deployment is a time-respecting split of reality, so shuffled-split benchmarks systematically overpromise, and the gap is measurable with data that already exists.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal splits are standard in some applied domains; a systematic audit across general vision benchmarks quantifying the shuffled-versus-temporal gap and its effect on model rankings may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify public vision datasets with usable timestamps, construct matched shuffled and temporal splits at equal sizes, train and evaluate a model panel on both, and report gap and ranking stability.
main_risk: Timestamps sometimes correlate with content or class balance changes, so drift attribution needs class-marginal controls to separate input drift from prior drift.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Within-dataset shuffling is treated as harmless because the data comes from one collection effort assumed homogeneous.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Cameras, platforms, content trends, and photographic conventions all change within multi-year collection windows, so homogeneity across time is an assumption contradicted by how the data was produced.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One timestamped dataset, earliest-third training and latest-third testing versus shuffled equivalent, one model, compare accuracies, one day.

one_line_idea: Near-duplicate structure in web-scale pretraining data inflates measured robustness because shifted test sets contain look-alikes of pretraining images.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web-scale pretraining corpora contain heavy near-duplicate structure, and popular shifted evaluation sets are themselves web-collected, creating potential overlap between pretraining neighborhoods and supposedly out-of-distribution test images.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable portion of foundation-model robustness on web-collected shift benchmarks is explained by near-duplicate or same-source proximity between test images and pretraining data, so robustness measured on proximity-filtered test subsets will be substantially lower.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying shifted test sets by embedding proximity to pretraining data will show accuracy declining sharply in the far strata, and models with different pretraining corpora will show different per-stratum profiles that track their corpus composition.
why_important: If robustness numbers partly measure pretraining-set recall, they overstate how models will handle genuinely novel conditions, which is the entire point of robustness evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contamination analysis exists for classification accuracy; proximity-stratified robustness measurement across shift benchmarks may be unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For models with inspectable pretraining corpora, compute test-image proximity to the corpus, stratify shifted-benchmark accuracy by proximity, and compare strata gaps across models and benchmarks.
main_risk: Proximity in embedding space conflates duplication with ordinary visual similarity, so duplicate detection thresholds must be validated on known-duplicate pairs.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Shifted benchmarks are treated as out-of-distribution for foundation models because they differ stylistically from canonical training sets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Out-of-distribution is relative to the pretraining corpus, not to a downstream dataset, and web-collected test sets are drawn from the same underlying pool as web-scale pretraining.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One open-corpus model, nearest-pretraining-neighbor distance for one shifted test set, accuracy in near versus far quartiles, one day.

one_line_idea: Realistic dependence structure in deployment streams breaks conformal prediction coverage for vision models, and the realized coverage gap is large enough to matter operationally.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Conformal prediction guarantees marginal coverage under exchangeability, and vision deployments violate exchangeability through temporal autocorrelation, bursts of related inputs, and feedback effects, yet conformal wrappers are promoted for deployment uncertainty.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under realistic vision-stream dependence, realized coverage of standard conformal methods deviates from nominal by operationally meaningful margins in stretches that matter, such as during bursts, even when long-run average coverage looks acceptable.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Replaying dependent streams built from real video, sessions, or temporally sorted data will show local coverage collapsing well below nominal during dependence bursts, with the deficit predicted by burst autocorrelation strength.
why_important: Users of conformal sets act on per-period reliability, and a method that holds on average while failing during exactly the correlated episodes when systems are stressed provides false assurance.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Non-exchangeable conformal theory exists; empirical quantification of local coverage failure on realistic vision streams, with burst-level analysis, may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct streams with graded dependence from video frames and session data, run standard and dependence-adjusted conformal methods, and report local coverage distributions rather than averages.
main_risk: Local coverage is itself a noisy quantity, and window-size choices for measuring it could exaggerate or hide the failures.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Conformal guarantees are perceived as distribution-free robustness that transfers to deployment with minor caveats.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The guarantee is conditional on exchangeability, which deployment streams violate structurally rather than marginally, and violated premises void the theorem exactly when correlations spike.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Calibrate conformal on shuffled frames, deploy on ordered video, measure coverage in sliding windows, hours.

one_line_idea: Photographer intent biases class-conditional distributions toward prototypical views, and models inherit a prototype bias that surfaces as viewpoint and context fragility under deployment shift.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dataset images are created by humans who choose subjects, angles, and moments deliberately, so the class-conditional distribution in datasets reflects photographic convention rather than the natural distribution of appearances a deployed camera encounters.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The gap between intent-curated and naturally sampled appearance distributions is a major unmodeled component of deployment shift, and models trained on intent-curated data will show accuracy drops on unposed captures that exceed drops predicted by standard low-level shift measures.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing model accuracy on deliberately captured versus passively captured images of identical object classes and scenes will show substantial gaps unexplained by image-quality covariates, concentrated in non-canonical viewpoints and partial visibility.
why_important: Passive capture, from wearables to vehicles to robots, is the growth area of vision deployment, and the intent bias hypothesis predicts systematic failure exactly there.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Viewpoint fragility is documented; framing photographer intent as a quantifiable sampling bias with matched-scene passive-capture comparison may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect or reuse matched deliberate and passive captures of the same scenes and classes, evaluate a model panel, and regress the accuracy gap on quality covariates to isolate the intent component.
main_risk: Matched-scene passive data is scarce, and quality covariates may not fully separate intent effects from capture-hardware effects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dataset class-conditionals are treated as reasonable samples of how objects appear, with viewpoint issues seen as a minor augmentation problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every dataset image passed a human filter for being worth capturing, and that filter is a strong non-random selection on appearance that deployment cameras do not apply.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare model accuracy on egocentric passive frames versus curated photos for shared object classes, controlling for resolution and blur, one day.

one_line_idea: A measurable share of reported distribution-shift degradation is actually annotation-standard shift, where label conventions rather than images changed between source and target.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Cross-dataset and cross-era evaluations attribute accuracy drops to input distribution change, but datasets also differ in labeling guidelines, taxonomy granularity, and annotator populations, which alter the ground truth itself.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For popular cross-dataset shift evaluations, relabeling a sample of target data under the source labeling standard will recover a substantial fraction of the reported accuracy drop, showing that part of the measured robustness gap is a measurement artifact of inconsistent ground truth.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Dual-standard relabeling studies will show model accuracy against source-standard labels significantly exceeding accuracy against native target labels on the same images, with the difference varying by class in ways that track guideline divergence.
why_important: Robustness research calibrates methods against measured drops, and if part of the drop is label-standard noise, method comparisons are contaminated by a term no algorithm could or should fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label-error studies exist for single benchmarks; decomposing cross-dataset shift drops into input-shift and label-standard components via dual relabeling may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select a cross-dataset evaluation pair, relabel a stratified target sample under the source guideline with trained annotators, and compare model accuracy under both label standards.
main_risk: Relabeling is expensive and annotator training imperfect, so the label-standard effect estimate will carry meaningful uncertainty at affordable sample sizes.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Accuracy drops across datasets are read as pure model failure under input shift, with ground truth assumed consistent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Labeling guidelines are documents written independently by different groups, and there is no mechanism that would make their induced ground truths agree on boundary cases.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Relabel two hundred target images under source rules, recompute one model's accuracy both ways, compare gap to the reported shift drop, days including annotation.

one_line_idea: Shared-source structure within single datasets violates i.i.d. assumptions enough that cluster-aware resampling changes benchmark conclusions, not just error bars.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Web-collected datasets draw many images from the same websites, photographers, and events, and both train and test splits inherit this cluster structure, potentially placing near-siblings across the split boundary.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-split sibling leakage inflates measured accuracy and compresses measured differences between models of different capacity, so cluster-aware re-splitting will lower absolute numbers and re-order some model comparisons, particularly favoring models that generalize rather than memorize source-specific signatures.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-splitting popular benchmarks by estimated source cluster will reduce accuracy for all models with the reduction correlated to model capacity, and will change the sign of some published pairwise comparisons.
why_important: If split construction determines conclusions, benchmark results encode data-plumbing artifacts, and the fix, cluster-aware splitting, is cheap once the structure is estimated.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Leakage studies exist for duplicates; systematic source-cluster re-splitting of standard vision benchmarks with conclusion-level impact analysis may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate source clusters via metadata and embedding linkage, re-split benchmarks with clusters kept intact, retrain or re-evaluate a model panel, and diff conclusions against original splits.
main_risk: Cluster estimation errors could either manufacture or hide the effect, so sensitivity to linkage thresholds must be reported.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Random splits are assumed adequate because obvious duplicates were removed during dataset construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deduplication removes near-identical images but not stylistic and contextual siblings from shared sources, which still carry predictive signatures models can exploit.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, group test images by domain-of-origin metadata, compare model accuracy on images with versus without training-split siblings from the same source, one day.

one_line_idea: Foundation-model robustness gains on shift benchmarks are largely pretraining-coverage effects, and an explicit coverage audit deflates claimed robustness to genuine novelty.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Prior analyses have reported that pretraining data distribution, more than architecture or objective, drives out-of-distribution performance of image-text models, yet robustness results are still routinely presented as intrinsic model properties.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For most celebrated foundation-model robustness results, the shifted test distribution is well covered by pretraining data, and robustness measured against coverage-controlled shift strata will show ordinary, unremarkable degradation, reducing claimed robustness to a data-coverage bookkeeping fact.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Quantifying per-benchmark coverage of shifted test data under open pretraining corpora will explain the bulk of variance in effective robustness across benchmarks, and low-coverage strata will show degradation comparable to non-foundation baselines.
why_important: The distinction between being robust and having seen it before determines whether robustness transfers to genuinely new deployment conditions, which is the question buyers of these models actually have.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The data-centric explanation is established qualitatively; a quantitative coverage-stratified re-analysis of the standard robustness benchmark suite may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For open-corpus models, define coverage scores of shifted test sets under the pretraining distribution, stratify effective-robustness measurements by coverage, and test whether coverage explains cross-benchmark robustness variance.
main_risk: Coverage metrics based on embedding proximity are circular if the same model defines the embedding, requiring an independent reference model.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Foundation-model robustness is widely narrated as an emergent capability of scale rather than a reflection of what the pretraining crawl happened to contain.
why_it_might_be_wrong: No mechanism has been demonstrated by which a statistical learner outperforms on distributions it lacks exposure to, making coverage the default explanation until excluded.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One open-corpus model, coverage scores for two shift benchmarks, correlate per-class coverage with per-class robustness, one day.

one_line_idea: A time-travel evaluation using only imagery created after a model's data cutoff provides the first clean measurement of foundation-model robustness to genuine novelty.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Every static shift benchmark potentially overlaps a foundation model's undisclosed pretraining crawl, making it impossible to certify that measured robustness reflects generalization rather than exposure, and models have documented training-data cutoffs.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Robustness measured on post-cutoff imagery, including new products, events, aesthetics, and camera pipelines, will be systematically lower than robustness measured on standard benchmarks for the same models, and the gap will grow with time since cutoff.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Building evaluation sets from verifiably post-cutoff images will show effective-robustness scores dropping relative to standard benchmarks for the same model, with older-cutoff models showing larger drops on the same post-cutoff data.
why_important: Deployment always happens after training, so post-cutoff performance is the deployment-relevant quantity, and it is currently unmeasured for essentially all foundation models.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal holdout evaluation is used in other machine-learning areas; a maintained post-cutoff robustness evaluation for vision foundation models may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect images with verifiable post-cutoff provenance across matched categories, evaluate models of different cutoffs zero-shot, and compare degradation ordered by cutoff date.
main_risk: Post-cutoff collections differ from benchmarks in more than novelty, so matched-category and matched-quality controls are needed to isolate the temporal effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark robustness is assumed to be a stable model property that forecasts future performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The visual world is non-stationary and pretraining crawls capture a frozen slice of it, so exposure-driven performance must decay as the world moves past the cutoff.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Assemble recent images of objects and scenes that verifiably postdate one model's cutoff, compare accuracy to matched pre-cutoff categories, days including collection.

one_line_idea: Robustness loss under downstream fine-tuning is a smooth function of parameter movement from the pretrained point, giving a practical dial for the accuracy-robustness tradeoff.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fine-tuning foundation models on downstream tasks is known to reduce their out-of-distribution robustness relative to zero-shot or lightly adapted variants, but the field lacks a quantitative law relating how much fine-tuning to how much robustness loss.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Effective robustness declines monotonically and smoothly with a measure of parameter displacement from the pretrained checkpoint, approximately independent of which fine-tuning method produced the displacement, making displacement a sufficient statistic for robustness loss.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across fine-tuning methods, learning rates, and durations, plotting effective robustness against parameter displacement will collapse the points onto a single method-independent curve per backbone and shift family.
why_important: A displacement law would let practitioners budget robustness like a resource, choosing fine-tuning intensity with predictable robustness cost instead of discovering the loss after deployment.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The qualitative tradeoff is established, and interpolation methods exploit it; a quantitative method-independent collapse onto a displacement curve may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one backbone with several methods across intensity grids, measure displacement in a fixed norm and effective robustness on a shift battery, and test for curve collapse across methods.
main_risk: Naive parameter norms may not be the right displacement metric, and failure to collapse could reflect metric choice rather than absence of a law.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Robustness loss is attributed to specific fine-tuning choices, with each method assumed to have its own robustness profile.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If pretrained structure is what confers robustness, then distance from that structure, however produced, should be the quantity that governs its erosion.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, three fine-tuning intensities and two methods, plot robustness versus displacement, check monotone collapse, two days.

one_line_idea: Out-of-distribution performance saturates with model scale earlier than in-distribution performance, indicating that robustness is data-limited rather than capacity-limited.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Scaling analyses for vision models report in-distribution gains with size and data, but the scaling behavior of out-of-distribution performance is far less characterized, and robustness investments are often justified by appeals to scale.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At fixed pretraining data, out-of-distribution accuracy as a function of model size flattens earlier than in-distribution accuracy, so beyond a modest scale, additional parameters buy in-distribution polish but no robustness, and only data changes move the out-of-distribution ceiling.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Model-size sweeps at fixed data will show the out-of-distribution scaling exponent decaying to near zero while the in-distribution exponent remains positive, and data sweeps at fixed size will show the opposite pattern.
why_important: Organizations decide between bigger models and better data; a demonstrated asymmetry for robustness would redirect spending for any application where shift matters.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scaling laws for in-distribution loss are well studied; separated size-versus-data scaling exponents for out-of-distribution vision performance may be uncharted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use existing public checkpoint families spanning sizes at documented data scales, evaluate on shift batteries, and fit separate scaling curves for in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy.
main_risk: Public checkpoint families confound size with training-recipe changes, so controlled small-scale training may be needed to confirm the pattern causally.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scale is assumed to improve everything jointly, with robustness expected to follow in-distribution gains automatically.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Capacity determines how well a model fits what it sees, while shift performance depends on what it saw, and those are different bottlenecks with different scaling currencies.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One public model family with several sizes at same data, evaluate in-distribution and one shift battery, compare curve shapes, one day.

one_line_idea: Foundation models are relatively less robust to low-level sensor and compression shifts than smaller supervised models, and their celebrated robustness advantage is semantic-only.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Foundation-model robustness claims are built mostly on semantic and stylistic shift benchmarks, while deployment shift often consists of sensor changes, compression artifacts, and optics degradation that such benchmarks underrepresent.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Web-scale pretraining concentrates diversity in semantics and style but is homogeneous in imaging pipeline statistics, so foundation models will show robustness advantages on semantic shifts and reduced or reversed advantages on low-level imaging shifts relative to supervised baselines trained with heavy low-level augmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A shift-type-decomposed evaluation will show the foundation-versus-baseline robustness gap being large on semantic shifts, small or negative on sensor-pipeline shifts, producing a two-by-two pattern current single-number reporting conceals.
why_important: Cameras, codecs, and optics vary enormously across deployments, and if foundation models are ordinary or worse there, adopters relying on their robustness reputation face unpriced risk.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Robustness decomposition by shift type exists in fragments; a direct foundation-versus-supervised comparison stratified into semantic versus imaging-pipeline shifts may be unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble matched semantic-shift and imaging-shift batteries, evaluate foundation models and augmentation-trained supervised baselines at matched in-distribution accuracy, and compare gap structure across the two shift types.
main_risk: Matching in-distribution accuracy across such different model classes is difficult, and unmatched comparisons would confound the decomposition.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Foundation models are assumed more robust across the board, with robustness treated as a scalar property.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web images are overwhelmingly processed through a narrow set of consumer pipelines, so pipeline-level diversity in pretraining is plausibly lower than what targeted augmentation gives supervised models.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One foundation model and one augmented supervised model at similar clean accuracy, evaluate on stylistic shift versus raw sensor-noise and compression shift, compare gaps, one day.

one_line_idea: Measured robustness differences between zero-shot and probed versions of the same backbone show that the classification head, not the representation, drives much of the foundation-model robustness story.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Zero-shot classifiers built from text embeddings and linear probes trained on downstream labels sit on the same frozen representation, yet robustness comparisons across models rarely control for which head type produced the numbers.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The text-derived head encodes class structure independent of any downstream dataset's statistics while the probe head absorbs source-dataset biases, so a large share of the zero-shot robustness advantage is a head effect, and head-controlled comparisons will substantially shrink claimed representation-level robustness differences between models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Crossing representations with head types will show head choice explaining a comparable or larger share of out-of-distribution variance than backbone choice among strong models, with probe heads consistently sacrificing robustness for in-distribution fit.
why_important: Model-selection decisions and scientific claims about which pretraining approach is more robust are confounded if the head effect is not separated from the representation effect.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Zero-shot-versus-probe robustness gaps are known for individual models; a factorial head-times-representation variance decomposition across model families may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several backbones, build zero-shot, linear-probe, and regularized-probe heads on identical representations, evaluate on a shift battery, and decompose out-of-distribution variance into head and representation components.
main_risk: Probe training details such as regularization strength strongly affect probe robustness, so the probe condition must span a defensible hyperparameter range.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Robustness numbers are attributed to the pretrained representation, with the head treated as a thin, neutral readout.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The head is the only component that ever sees the downstream source distribution, making it the natural entry point for source-specific bias that fails under shift.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, zero-shot head versus linear probe on one downstream dataset, evaluate both on its shifted variants, compare robustness gap, hours.

one_line_idea: At matched pretraining data, contrastive, captioning, and self-supervised objectives yield similar distribution-shift robustness, showing that the objective is incidental and data is the whole story.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Robustness comparisons between models trained with different objectives are almost always confounded by different pretraining corpora, so the community's beliefs about which objective confers robustness rest on uncontrolled comparisons.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When pretraining data is held fixed, objective choice moves out-of-distribution robustness by only a small margin relative to the data effect, and reported objective-attributed robustness differences in the literature will mostly disappear under data-matched training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Data-matched pretraining runs across objectives at feasible scale will produce effective-robustness spreads across objectives much smaller than spreads across data compositions at fixed objective.
why_important: Objective design consumes significant research effort justified partly by robustness claims; establishing data primacy would refocus that effort on curation, which is cheaper and more controllable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-centric robustness evidence exists for specific families; a deliberate objective-versus-data factorial at matched scale for shift robustness may be unavailable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain models with several objectives on identical data and matched compute at moderate scale, evaluate on a shift battery, and compare objective-induced versus data-induced robustness spreads with a data-composition arm.
main_risk: Conclusions at feasible academic scale may not extrapolate to frontier scale where objectives could interact differently with capacity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Language-supervised contrastive training is often credited with special robustness properties relative to purely visual self-supervision.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The credited comparisons changed data and objective simultaneously, and the data changed by orders of magnitude more than the objective changed the learning signal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two objectives, one fixed medium-scale corpus, matched compute pretraining, one shift battery, compare robustness spread to a data-halving arm, several days of training.

one_line_idea: Robustness-intervention effects measured on small models predict their effects on foundation-scale models, enabling cheap screening before expensive integration.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Robustness interventions such as augmentation schemes, regularizers, and architectural tweaks are proposed continuously, but verifying each at foundation scale is unaffordable, so adoption decisions are made on faith or skipped.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The sign and approximate relative magnitude of an intervention's effect on shift robustness is preserved from small-scale to large-scale training within a model family, so a standardized small-scale screening battery predicts foundation-scale outcomes well enough to triage interventions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For a panel of interventions evaluated at several scales, small-scale robustness effects will rank-correlate strongly with large-scale effects, with prediction failures concentrated in interventions that interact with data diversity.
why_important: A validated screening protocol would industrialize robustness research, replacing anecdotal adoption with cheap systematic triage, and identifying where scale genuinely changes conclusions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scale transfer of architecture and hyperparameter decisions is studied for accuracy; a transferability study specifically for robustness interventions may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select a panel of published interventions, train with and without each at three scales in one family, measure shift-robustness effects per scale, and evaluate cross-scale rank prediction.
main_risk: If effects are small relative to seed noise at small scale, screening power collapses and the protocol would need many seeds to be informative.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Robustness findings at small scale are widely distrusted for foundation-scale relevance, so they are neither systematically produced nor used.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Many interventions act through scale-independent mechanisms such as input statistics diversification, and such mechanisms should transfer even when absolute numbers do not.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three interventions at two small scales, check whether the robustness-effect ordering is preserved across the scale step, several days.

one_line_idea: Background and texture shortcut reliance survives foundation-model scale essentially unchanged; scale reduces failure frequency but not the failure mechanism.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Shortcut learning, such as classifying by background or texture, was documented extensively for supervised networks, and foundation models are often presumed to have transcended it due to data scale and language supervision.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation models rely on the same shortcut features when discriminative foreground evidence weakens, so controlled foreground-background recombination tests will show the same qualitative failure pattern as older models, with only the threshold shifted.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On composited images placing objects on incongruent backgrounds with graded foreground degradation, foundation models will show background-driven predictions emerging at some degradation level for most classes, mirroring supervised-model curves shifted rightward but not qualitatively different.
why_important: If the failure mechanism persists, scale bought a margin rather than a fix, and safety-critical use still requires shortcut-specific defenses that current robustness narratives suggest are obsolete.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Shortcut studies at foundation scale exist in scattered forms; graded-evidence threshold curves comparing model generations under one protocol may be unavailable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build composited evaluation sets with controllable foreground evidence strength and incongruent backgrounds, evaluate model generations, and compare background-reliance threshold curves.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts could themselves drive predictions, so real photographed incongruent scenes should anchor a subset of the evaluation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scale plus diverse pretraining is assumed to have largely eliminated crude shortcut reliance in frontier vision models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shortcuts exist because they are statistically valid in training distributions, and web-scale data preserves rather than removes those correlations, so the learning incentive is unchanged.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifty composited incongruent-background images with weak foregrounds, run one frontier model, count background-consistent predictions, hours.

one_line_idea: Retrieval and classification robustness of the same vision-language model diverge under identical shifts, so single-task robustness certification is misleading for multi-use foundation models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Foundation models are deployed simultaneously for classification, retrieval, captioning, and matching, but robustness is certified almost exclusively via classification benchmarks, with the implicit assumption that robustness transfers across usage modes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Different usage modes stress different properties of the representation, so a shift that leaves classification accuracy intact can severely degrade retrieval quality of the same model on the same data, and vice versa, making task-conditional robustness profiles necessary.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating one model across usage modes under identical shifts will reveal mode-shift interactions, with rank correlation between per-shift classification degradation and per-shift retrieval degradation substantially below one.
why_important: Organizations certify a model once and deploy it many ways, and a divergence between mode robustness means the certification does not cover actual usage.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Task-specific robustness is studied per task; within-model cross-mode robustness divergence under matched shifts may be uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a model and a shift battery, evaluate classification, retrieval, and matching metrics on identical shifted data, and quantify per-shift degradation correlation across modes.
main_risk: Metrics across modes are not directly comparable, so degradation must be normalized carefully, for example by matched clean-performance percentiles.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A robust model is assumed robust as a representation, with task wiring treated as irrelevant to its shift behavior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Classification uses a few discriminative directions while retrieval depends on the full metric structure of the embedding space, and shifts can damage either one selectively.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one corruption battery, measure zero-shot classification and image-to-image retrieval degradation on the same images, compare orderings, hours.

one_line_idea: Instruction tuning and preference alignment of vision-language assistants degrade the distribution-shift robustness of their underlying visual competence, an unmeasured robustness tax.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-language assistants are built by further tuning base models on curated instruction and preference data, which is far narrower in visual distribution than pretraining, and their robustness is rarely compared against their own base models.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The narrowing of visual data during alignment stages pulls visual representations toward the instruction-data distribution, so assistant variants will show larger shifted-input degradation than their base models on matched visual tasks, with the tax growing across successive alignment stages.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stage-wise evaluation of model lineages from base through instruction-tuned to preference-tuned checkpoints will show monotone or near-monotone decline in visual shift robustness at matched clean performance.
why_important: Assistants are the deployment surface through which most users now consume vision capabilities, and an alignment robustness tax means the deployed products are less robust than the benchmarks of their bases suggest.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Alignment effects on language behavior are studied; lineage-resolved visual robustness tracking across tuning stages may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain public model lineages with released intermediate checkpoints, evaluate each stage on shifted visual tasks at matched clean accuracy, and track robustness across stages.
main_risk: Interface differences between base and assistant models complicate matched evaluation, requiring careful task formatting to avoid measuring prompt-handling rather than vision.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Alignment is assumed to affect style and safety while leaving core visual competence untouched.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tuning stages continue updating shared parameters on visually narrow data, and continued training on narrow distributions is the canonical mechanism of robustness loss.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One public base-and-assistant pair, matched visual question set clean versus corrupted, compare degradation ratios, one day.

one_line_idea: Averaging weights of independently fine-tuned models recovers more of the robustness lost to fine-tuning than any specialized robust-training objective, at zero inference cost.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fine-tuning erodes foundation-model robustness, and the proposed remedies include specialized objectives, regularizers toward pretrained weights, and weight-space interpolation, but these families are rarely compared head-to-head at matched budgets.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Weight averaging across independently fine-tuned runs dominates specialized robust-fine-tuning objectives on the robustness-accuracy frontier, because run diversity captures complementary solutions while objectives merely constrain a single trajectory.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At matched total compute, averaged ensembles of plainly fine-tuned models will Pareto-dominate specialized robust objectives on in-distribution accuracy versus out-of-distribution accuracy across most tested shift families.
why_important: If the best remedy is an embarrassingly simple procedure, robust-fine-tuning research needs rebasing against it, and practitioners get an immediately deployable default.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Weight averaging and robust objectives are separately established; a budget-matched frontier comparison framing averaging as the incumbent to beat may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune a backbone with plain training multiple times and with robust objectives at matched compute, form averaged variants, and map the accuracy-robustness frontier across all configurations.
main_risk: Averaging requires runs to remain in compatible loss basins, and aggressive fine-tuning settings could break averaging in ways that flatter the objective-based methods.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Robust fine-tuning is treated as an objective-design problem, with averaging seen as an orthogonal trick rather than the benchmark to beat.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging exploits solution diversity that no single-trajectory objective can access, and diversity is the standard mechanism behind robustness gains from ensembling.
