fastest_falsification_experiment: Three plain fine-tuning runs averaged versus one robust-objective run at triple length, compare frontier points on two shifts, two days.

one_line_idea: Method rankings from synthetic corruption benchmarks do not transfer to natural distribution shifts, and continued use of corruptions as the primary robustness certification is quantitatively unjustified.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Prior work has reported weak relationships between synthetic-corruption robustness and natural-shift robustness for some model classes, yet corruption suites remain the field's default robustness certification and the primary target of new methods.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across a broad modern method panel, per-method gains on corruption suites will explain little of the variance in gains on natural shifts, and methods materially reorder between the two regimes, meaning the field's primary instrument mismeasures its stated goal.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating many published robustness methods on both corruption suites and a battery of natural shifts will yield low cross-regime rank correlation of gains, with specialized corruption methods showing the largest regressions on natural shift.
why_important: Certification instruments shape method development; quantifying the transfer failure at panel scale either retires the instrument or defines its valid scope.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The concern is documented for model robustness; a method-level gain-transfer analysis across the current robustness-method literature may be unassembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reproduce a panel of robustness methods on one backbone, evaluate gains on corruption suites and natural-shift sets, and report cross-regime correlation with per-method scatter.
main_risk: Natural-shift batteries embed their own idiosyncrasies, so several independent natural shifts are needed to claim regime-level conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Corruption-suite gains are still routinely presented and accepted as evidence of general robustness improvement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Corruptions perturb pixels while natural shifts change scene composition and populations, and methods optimized for the former have no mechanism to address the latter.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three corruption-oriented methods, one natural geographic shift set, check whether corruption gains predict natural gains, one day.

one_line_idea: Benchmark domains are confounded bundles of style, content, and class-balance factors, and factorized shift benchmarks would reattribute much of what the field calls domain gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark domains such as photo versus sketch differ simultaneously in rendering style, object poses, background presence, and class frequencies, and reported domain gaps aggregate all of these into one number attributed to style.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Decomposing existing benchmark domain gaps by controlling factors one at a time will show that class balance and content composition explain a large share of measured gaps, with pure rendering style a smaller contributor than assumed, changing which methods look effective.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Factor-controlled re-evaluations, matching class balance and content statistics across domains before measuring residual gaps, will shrink measured domain gaps substantially and reorder method effectiveness on the residual style-only component.
why_important: Methods are designed against what benchmarks say the problem is; if the problem is misattributed, method design has been aimed at the wrong factor for years.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Factor confounding in domain benchmarks is occasionally acknowledged; an executed factor-decomposition of the standard benchmark suite may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For each benchmark pair, construct class-balance-matched and content-matched subsets, measure per-factor gap contributions, and re-evaluate representative methods on the residual factor.
main_risk: Matching on some factors reduces sample sizes sharply, and small residual sets may be too noisy for method comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Benchmark domain gaps are interpreted as measuring style or appearance shift, since domains are named after visual styles.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Simple checks show class distributions differ markedly across benchmark domains, and class-frequency mismatch alone mechanically produces accuracy gaps without any style effect.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark pair, recompute the domain gap after class-balance matching alone, compare to the published gap, hours.

one_line_idea: Popular web-scraped shift test sets are inside foundation-model pretraining distributions, and a decontamination protocol is required before any foundation-model robustness number on them is meaningful.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Widely used shifted test sets containing renditions, sketches, and unusual examples were scraped from the same web that foundation-model pretraining crawls cover, and pretraining corpora for most frontier models are undisclosed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Overlap between such test sets and pretraining neighborhoods is extensive enough that foundation-model scores on them measure exposure rather than robustness, and proximity-based decontamination will reduce measured robustness substantially and non-uniformly across models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For models with open corpora, removing test images whose pretraining neighborhoods are close will lower shifted-set accuracy well beyond the effect of equal-sized random removal, and model rankings will change after decontamination.
why_important: These test sets anchor the narrative of emergent foundation-model robustness, and contamination would mean the narrative rests on recycled training data.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Contamination auditing is active for language evaluation; a rigorous decontamination protocol and re-scoring for vision shift benchmarks may be unbuilt.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Using open-corpus models, compute pretraining-neighborhood proximity for shifted test images, re-score accuracy on decontaminated subsets against random-removal controls, and compare model rankings before and after.
main_risk: Proximity thresholds are contestable, and results must be presented as curves over threshold rather than single numbers to be credible.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Shifted test sets are treated as fair out-of-distribution probes for all models regardless of pretraining provenance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A test image sitting near pretraining data is in-distribution by definition for that model, whatever the benchmark's name says.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One open-corpus model, one rendition-style test set, accuracy on nearest-neighbor-close versus far halves, one day.

one_line_idea: As in-distribution accuracy saturates, effective-robustness slopes become statistically unidentifiable, and the field needs harder in-distribution benchmarks merely to keep measuring robustness.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Effective-robustness analysis fits trends between in-distribution and shifted accuracy across models, and frontier models now cluster within a narrow band near the top of standard in-distribution benchmarks.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] With in-distribution scores compressed into a narrow range, the leverage needed to estimate robustness trends vanishes, so recent claims of above-trend robustness for frontier models are statistically fragile and sensitive to a handful of points.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Reanalysis of current model collections with proper uncertainty on trend fits will show that above-the-line claims for many frontier models lose significance, and that simulated harder benchmarks restore identifiability by decompressing the in-distribution axis.
why_important: Robustness science depends on this measurement tool, and using it beyond its valid range produces confident but meaningless conclusions about which models are genuinely robust.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Effective robustness is widely used; an identifiability analysis of the methodology under score saturation may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take published model collections, bootstrap trend fits with model resampling, quantify uncertainty of above-trend residuals for top models, and repeat on synthetic decompressed axes to show recoverability.
main_risk: Bootstrap over correlated model families understates uncertainty, so family structure must be respected in resampling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Effective-robustness plots are read at face value, with position above the trend line accepted as evidence of robustness gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fitting a slope requires spread in the predictor, and the predictor's spread among relevant models has collapsed by an order of magnitude since the methodology was introduced.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Bootstrap the trend fit on a published model collection restricted to frontier models, check whether above-line residuals retain significance, hours.

one_line_idea: Static shift benchmarks cannot rank methods for real gradual drift; stream benchmarks with controlled drift dynamics reverse adaptation-method rankings.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real deployment drift is gradual, autocorrelated, and sometimes cyclic, while benchmarks present shift as a static before-and-after comparison, and adaptation methods are ranked on the static version.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Method performance depends strongly on drift dynamics such as speed, smoothness, and cyclicity, so rankings from static benchmarks will fail to predict rankings under realistic dynamics, with dynamics-aware simple methods overtaking static-benchmark leaders.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A benchmark generator interpolating between distributions at controlled speeds will show method rankings varying strongly with drift speed, and static-benchmark rankings matching only the near-instantaneous-drift corner of the space.
why_important: If rankings are dynamics-dependent, the field's league tables answer a corner case, and method choice for real systems is effectively unguided.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Continual shift datasets exist; a parameterized drift-dynamics generator with ranking-stability analysis across the dynamics space may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build drift streams by interpolating existing domain pairs at several speeds and cyclicity patterns, evaluate adaptation methods across the dynamics grid, and map ranking stability.
main_risk: Interpolation-generated intermediates may be unrealistic, so at least one naturally time-stamped stream should validate the generator's conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Static-benchmark rankings are used as general guidance for method selection under any drift pattern.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptation methods embody assumptions about how much past data resembles the present, which is precisely what drift dynamics control, so dynamics-dependent rankings are the expected geometry of the problem.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One domain pair, three interpolation speeds, three methods, check ranking stability across speeds, one day.

one_line_idea: Geographic-shift benchmark degradation conflates image-distribution change with label-taxonomy mismatch across regions, and region-relabeled evaluation would separate the two.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmarks measuring performance across countries and regions report large accuracy drops attributed to visual distribution shift, but category definitions themselves, such as which objects count as a stove or a shop, vary culturally across regions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial component of measured geographic degradation is taxonomy mismatch rather than visual unfamiliarity, so evaluating with region-adapted label mappings will recover a meaningful fraction of the reported drop without touching the model.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructing region-aware label mappings with local annotators and re-scoring existing model predictions will reduce measured geographic gaps noticeably, with the reduction varying by category in proportion to cultural variability of the category definition.
why_important: The geographic-robustness literature drives both research and policy claims about model fairness across regions, and conflated measurement distorts both the size and the nature of the problem.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Geographic performance gaps are well documented; decomposition into visual-shift versus taxonomy-mismatch components via region-adapted relabeling may be undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one geographic benchmark, build region-adapted answer keys for a category sample with local annotation, re-score frozen model predictions under both keys, and attribute the gap components.
main_risk: Region-adapted keys could be accused of moving the goalposts, so the mapping construction must be pre-registered and independent of model outputs.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Geographic accuracy gaps are interpreted as models failing to recognize unfamiliar visual environments.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A model that correctly identifies a regional object variant can still be scored wrong if the benchmark key encodes another region's category conventions, and nothing in current scoring rules this out.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Manually audit one hundred errors of one model on a geographic benchmark, count cases where the prediction is locally defensible under a region-aware reading, days including annotation.

one_line_idea: No robustness method Pareto-dominates across shift types, and shift-type profiles should replace single-number robustness leaderboards.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Robustness papers report averaged scores across heterogeneous shift collections, producing single-number comparisons and state-of-the-art claims that imply uniform superiority.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Method gains are strongly shift-type-specific with pervasive trade-offs, so across a broad method panel virtually no method will dominate another on all shift families, and averaged leaderboards mask anticorrelated specializations.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A per-family re-analysis of published methods will show most method pairs exhibiting reversed orderings across at least one pair of shift families, and average-score leaders failing to lead in most individual families.
why_important: Deployment involves specific expected shifts, and a profile tells a practitioner what to use, while an average tells them almost nothing and rewards benchmark-portfolio tuning.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Per-dataset numbers exist inside papers; a cross-literature dominance analysis formalizing the no-dominance claim may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble per-shift-family results for a broad method panel via reproduction, compute pairwise dominance relations across families, and quantify the prevalence of trade-offs.
main_risk: Reproduction noise could manufacture apparent trade-offs, so per-family differences must be tested against seed variance before counting reversals.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Averaged robustness scores are treated as a meaningful total ordering of methods, sustaining state-of-the-art claims.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Different shift families have close to orthogonal causes, and a single intervention improving all of them simultaneously would be mechanistically surprising.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Five methods with published per-dataset numbers, build the dominance matrix across shift families, count reversals, hours with published data plus verification.

one_line_idea: Subpopulation-shift benchmarks overstate the availability of group labels, and under realistic group-label-free conditions the reported superiority of group-robust methods over plain training shrinks or vanishes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Group-robustness benchmarks supply annotated group labels for training or validation, and leading methods consume them, while real deployments rarely have reliable group annotation at any stage.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The advantage of group-robust methods is concentrated in their privileged access to group labels for model selection, so under a strict no-group-information protocol, including selection, their worst-group performance advantage over well-tuned plain training will largely disappear.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-running benchmark suites under a no-group-labels-anywhere protocol will compress the gap between group-robust methods and plain training with strong regularization, with remaining differences within selection noise for most datasets.
why_important: Practitioners without group labels need to know whether these methods offer them anything, and the benchmarks as configured cannot answer that question.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The role of group-labeled validation is acknowledged in parts of the literature; a strict full-pipeline no-group-information audit across the benchmark suite may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a protocol forbidding group labels in training and selection, re-run representative methods and strong plain baselines across standard subpopulation benchmarks, and compare worst-group accuracy distributions.
main_risk: Worst-group evaluation itself requires group labels, which is legitimate for measurement, but leakage through repeated evaluation-informed development must be guarded against.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Group-robust methods are believed to substantially beat plain training on subpopulation shift, as leaderboards configured with group labels indicate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Selection on worst-group validation accuracy is a powerful optimizer, and granting it exclusively to some methods is an uncontrolled advantage unrelated to their stated mechanisms.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One benchmark, one group-robust method versus tuned plain training, both selected without group labels, compare worst-group accuracy, one day.

one_line_idea: Adversarially-filtered hard test sets measure disagreement with the filter model rather than distribution shift, and robustness conclusions drawn from them are filter-relative artifacts.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Several benchmark test sets were constructed by keeping only examples that a reference model misclassified, a procedure that couples the test distribution to one particular model's failure surface.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Performance on filter-constructed sets is dominated by a model's representational similarity to the filter model rather than by robustness to any natural distribution, so scores on such sets will be predictable from model-filter similarity and will misrank models relative to unfiltered hard-case evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a model panel, similarity to the filter model in error-pattern space will strongly predict filtered-set accuracy, and rankings on filtered sets will diverge from rankings on naturally hard unfiltered data matched for difficulty.
why_important: These sets are cited as evidence of natural-distribution brittleness, and if they encode filter artifacts, both the brittleness narrative and method progress measured on them need reinterpretation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Selection-bias critiques of filtered sets exist; a quantitative filter-similarity analysis explaining panel-wide score variance may be unavailable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute error-pattern similarity of each panel model to the filter model on neutral data, correlate with filtered-set scores, and compare rankings against difficulty-matched unfiltered hard sets.
main_risk: Constructing difficulty-matched unfiltered comparison sets is hard, and mismatched difficulty would contaminate the ranking comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Filtered hard sets are treated as neutral probes of natural robustness applicable to all models equally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Conditioning a test set on one model's errors mathematically ties the set to that model's decision boundary, a dependence that does not fade as other models improve.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ten models, correlate filtered-set accuracy with agreement-with-filter-model on neutral data, check correlation strength, one day.

one_line_idea: Robustness benchmark numbers are unstable to preprocessing details at magnitudes comparable to published method gains, and a preprocessing-sensitivity audit is a missing requirement.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Shifted-set evaluation involves resizing, cropping, interpolation, and normalization choices that vary across codebases, and shifted images interact with preprocessing differently than clean images, for example corruptions interacting with downsampling filters.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Reasonable preprocessing variations move shifted-set accuracy by margins comparable to typical claimed method improvements, and some published cross-paper comparisons are dominated by unreported preprocessing differences rather than methods.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A sensitivity sweep over defensible preprocessing configurations will show shifted-set accuracy varying by more than the median published method gain on the same benchmarks, with corruption-style sets most sensitive.
why_important: If the measurement instrument has error bars wider than the effects being claimed, the literature's incremental comparisons need preprocessing standardization before they are interpretable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Preprocessing effects are known folklore; a quantified sensitivity audit sized against the distribution of published gains may be absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix models, sweep interpolation methods, resize orders, crop ratios, and compression settings within accepted practice, measure shifted-set accuracy spread, and compare to a survey of published method gains.
main_risk: Defining the space of reasonable preprocessing is subjective, and an overly broad space would exaggerate the instability.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Preprocessing is assumed standardized enough that cross-paper robustness comparisons reflect methods rather than pipelines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shift benchmarks specifically alter low-level statistics, which is exactly the regime where preprocessing choices change what the network receives most.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model, one corruption set, three interpolation modes and two resize orders, measure accuracy spread, hours.

one_line_idea: Caching and re-using per-condition adapters, a domain memory, beats continual gradient updating under recurring shift conditions and eliminates catastrophic forgetting by construction.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Deployment conditions recur, day follows night and seasons cycle, yet continual test-time adaptation methods re-learn each condition from scratch on every visit while fighting forgetting of previous states.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Maintaining a library of lightweight condition-specific adapter states, with unsupervised retrieval of the matching adapter per input batch, outperforms continual updating on recurring streams because retrieval replaces re-learning and isolation prevents interference.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On streams with recurring conditions, the adapter-library approach will show higher time-averaged accuracy than continual-updating methods, with the advantage growing in the number of revisits and vanishing on non-recurring streams.
why_important: Recurrence is the dominant structure of real drift, and a mechanism that exploits it converts the hardest part of continual adaptation, forgetting, into a non-problem.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Modular and mixture approaches exist in continual learning; an unsupervised retrieval-based adapter memory for test-time adaptation on recurring streams may be unexplored territory.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement adapter caching keyed by embedding statistics, compare against continual methods on constructed recurring streams and one naturally cyclic stream, and measure time-averaged accuracy versus revisit count.
main_risk: Unsupervised condition retrieval may misfire near condition boundaries, and retrieval errors could cost more than continual updating loses to forgetting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Continual adaptation is framed as a plasticity-stability optimization within a single parameter state, not as a routing-and-memory problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Storing solutions is strictly easier than re-deriving them, and condition identity is low-dimensional and cheap to infer relative to full adaptation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Alternating two-condition stream, cache-and-retrieve two adapters versus one continual method, compare time-averaged accuracy, one day.

one_line_idea: The optimal adaptation learning rate under gradual drift is a function of measurable drift speed, and an adaptive-rate law derived from it beats every fixed-rate configuration.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Online adaptation methods use fixed learning rates chosen by benchmark tuning, while drift in deployments varies in speed over time, and rate misconfiguration causes either lag behind the drift or noise amplification.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] There is a stable functional relationship between drift speed, estimable from windowed embedding statistics, and the regret-minimizing adaptation rate, so a controller that sets the rate from estimated speed will approach oracle-rate performance across drift regimes without per-deployment tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across streams spanning slow, fast, and varying drift, the speed-tracking controller will match the best fixed rate in each regime and beat every single fixed rate on the mixed regime, approaching the oracle schedule within a small margin.
why_important: Rate selection is the main deployment-blocking hyperparameter of online adaptation, and replacing it with a measurement-driven law removes the need for per-site tuning that no operator can perform.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Drift-adaptive step sizes exist in online learning theory; an empirically validated speed-to-rate law for deep vision adaptation with drift-speed estimation from embeddings may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate drift streams with controlled speeds, sweep fixed rates to map the oracle rate per speed, fit the speed-to-rate relationship, then validate the controller on held-out mixed-speed streams.
main_risk: Drift-speed estimation from embeddings may confuse drift with noise bursts, and a controller reacting to noise would amplify exactly what it should damp.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adaptation rates are treated as method constants to be benchmarked once, rather than as quantities that must track a property of the environment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tracking theory in simpler settings makes the optimal rate scale with the drift-to-noise ratio, and there is no reason deep adaptation escapes that structural dependence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three drift speeds, five fixed rates, verify the optimal rate shifts with speed and a two-point controller interpolation beats fixed rates on a mixed stream, one day.

one_line_idea: Long-horizon stability of online adaptation is governed by the dimensionality of the updated parameter subspace, and full-parameter online updating diverges with probability approaching one.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Online adaptation methods differ in what they update, from normalization scales through prompts and low-rank adapters to all weights, and stability comparisons across these choices are anecdotal rather than systematic.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Divergence risk on unbounded unlabeled streams grows sharply with updated-subspace dimensionality at fixed step size, producing a stability-capacity frontier where low-dimensional updates are stable but expressivity-limited and full updates are expressive but almost surely divergent over long horizons.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping updated-subspace size across orders of magnitude on long streams will show time-to-divergence decreasing systematically with dimensionality, with a measurable frontier that shifts but does not disappear under stronger regularization.
why_important: The frontier would give deployment engineering a concrete design rule, choose the largest subspace whose divergence horizon exceeds the reset schedule, replacing folklore about which parameters are safe to touch.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Parameter-subset choices are compared for accuracy in papers; a systematic stability-versus-dimensionality characterization on long unlabeled streams may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix one adaptation objective, vary only the updated parameter set across normalization, prompts, low-rank, and full weights, run long streams with multiple seeds, and record divergence statistics per dimensionality.
main_risk: Divergence depends jointly on step size and dimensionality, so the frontier must be mapped over both axes to avoid confounded conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Restricting updates to small parameter subsets is seen as a compute convenience rather than the primary determinant of long-run stability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Unsupervised objectives have degenerate optima, and the volume of parameter space from which updates can reach degeneracy grows with the dimensionality of what is free to move.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Entropy objective with normalization-only versus full-parameter updates on a stream fifty times standard length, three seeds, compare divergence counts, one day.

one_line_idea: A divergence anchor to the frozen source model replaces stored source data in online adaptation, giving replay-level stability at zero storage and no privacy cost.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Stability mechanisms for online adaptation often rely on replaying stored source examples or statistics, which costs memory and is impossible under privacy constraints that prohibit retaining training data.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The stabilizing content of source replay is the anchoring of predictions near source behavior on non-shifted inputs, which a prediction-divergence penalty against the frozen source copy provides equivalently, so anchored adaptation will match replay-based stability across long streams without any stored data.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On long non-stationary streams, anchored adaptation will match replay-based variants in both time-averaged accuracy and post-stream source-task retention, while pure unanchored adaptation degrades on both metrics.
why_important: Replay-free stability makes online adaptation deployable in privacy-regulated settings, which include most medical, surveillance, and consumer contexts where adaptation is most needed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Distillation-style anchors appear in continual learning; a controlled equivalence claim between source replay and frozen-copy anchoring for unlabeled test-time adaptation may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement matched adaptation pipelines differing only in stabilizer, source replay versus frozen-copy divergence penalty versus none, and compare accuracy and retention across long shift sequences.
main_risk: The anchor pulls toward source behavior on all inputs including genuinely shifted ones, potentially capping adaptation gains in ways replay does not.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Access to source data or its statistics is considered a meaningful advantage for stabilizing adaptation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The frozen model is a compressed representative of the source data for exactly the function being stabilized, so the data itself may add nothing the copy does not already provide.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One shift sequence, anchored versus replay-stabilized adaptation with matched budgets, compare end-of-stream accuracy and source retention, one day.

one_line_idea: Test-time adaptation methods silently assume covariate shift, and under label-conditional drift they confidently adapt in the wrong direction, making things worse than no adaptation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Unsupervised adaptation objectives operate on inputs and model predictions without labels, and their validity arguments implicitly assume the input-to-label relationship is stable while only input marginals change.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When the conditional relationship drifts, as in changed visual conventions or evolving category usage, the same objectives that help under covariate shift produce systematically harmful updates, and the harm scales with adaptation strength, creating a regime where stronger methods are strictly worse.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On constructed streams where the label function changes for a subset of classes, adaptation methods will amplify errors on those classes relative to the frozen model, with per-class harm proportional to the method's update magnitude.
why_important: Deployments cannot verify which shift type they face, so a method family that is helpful under one type and harmful under the sibling type is unsafe without a discriminating diagnostic, which does not currently exist.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Covariate-shift assumptions are stated in theory sections; empirical quantification of adaptation harm under controlled conditional drift in vision streams may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct streams mixing covariate shift with controlled conditional changes by relabeling protocols or naturally re-annotated data, run adaptation methods at several strengths, and measure per-class harm against the frozen baseline.
main_risk: Constructing believable conditional drift in vision requires care, and artificial relabeling could be dismissed as unrealistic without a natural example to anchor it.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Unsupervised adaptation is regarded as low-risk on the grounds that unlabeled data cannot mislead about labels.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Confidence-based objectives reinforce the model's current input-label mapping, which is precisely the wrong move when that mapping is what changed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Swap the definition of two visually similar classes midstream, run one adaptation method, watch error amplification on the swapped classes, hours.

one_line_idea: Self-supervised test-time training helps only when the auxiliary task is statistically coupled to the shift, and a computable coupling diagnostic predicts its sign of effect.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Test-time training updates features through an auxiliary self-supervised task on test inputs, and reported results show it helping on some shifts while being neutral or harmful on others without a predictive account of which occurs when.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The effect of test-time training is governed by the correlation between auxiliary-task gradients and the gradients that would reduce main-task error under the specific shift, so a coupling coefficient estimated from labeled probe shifts predicts the sign and rough size of the benefit on new shifts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across a battery of shifts, the measured auxiliary-to-main gradient alignment will separate positive-benefit from negative-benefit cases with high accuracy, and shifts orthogonal to the auxiliary task will cluster at zero benefit.
why_important: A validity predictor converts an unreliable technique into a deployable one by gating it, and clarifies the mechanism behind a widely cited but inconsistently reproduced method family.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Task-coupling explanations have been theorized in restricted models; an empirical coupling diagnostic validated across shift families on modern backbones may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For each shift in a battery, measure gradient alignment between auxiliary and main objectives on small labeled probes, run test-time training, and correlate realized benefit with measured alignment.
main_risk: Gradient alignment measured at the initial point may not reflect alignment along the whole adaptation trajectory, weakening the diagnostic for long adaptation runs.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Self-supervised test-time training is presented as broadly applicable, with failures attributed to tuning rather than to structural task mismatch.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Updating features to satisfy an auxiliary task can only help the main task through shared structure, and when the shift damages structure the auxiliary task does not see, no mechanism connects the update to the harm.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two shifts chosen to plausibly differ in coupling, measure alignment and run test-time training on both, check sign agreement, one day.

one_line_idea: Online adaptation methods are broken by realistic non-uniform arrival processes such as class bursts, and arrival-robustness should be a first-class evaluation axis.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real input streams arrive with strong temporal structure, bursts of similar content, session effects, and diurnal cycles, while adaptation benchmarks feed methods class-balanced shuffled batches.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Popular adaptation methods implicitly rely on within-window class diversity, so realistic bursty arrival will cause prior-collapse updates and accuracy loss even with zero distribution shift, and method rankings under bursty arrival will differ sharply from shuffled-arrival rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Replaying identical data in shuffled versus bursty orders will produce large accuracy differences for adaptation methods but not for frozen models, with some methods degraded below the frozen baseline purely by arrival order.
why_important: Arrival structure is universal in deployment and free to simulate in evaluation, so ignoring it inflates reported reliability at no benefit.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporally correlated test streams appear in a few papers; arrival-order robustness as a systematic evaluation axis with burst-parameterized stress tests may be unestablished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix datasets and shifts, replay streams under parameterized arrival processes varying burst length and class concentration, and measure each method's accuracy as a function of arrival parameters.
main_risk: Bursty replay changes the effective local distribution, so the analysis must separate arrival-order effects from genuine local-distribution effects with frozen-model controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Shuffled arrival is treated as a neutral simplification rather than an assumption doing load-bearing work in reported results.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Objectives that sharpen predictions toward the recent window's statistics will chase bursts by design, and burst-chasing is indistinguishable from prior collapse at the update level.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One method, same corrupted data replayed shuffled versus sorted-by-class, compare accuracy trajectories, hours.

one_line_idea: Under matched compute budgets, simple adaptation baselines beat sophisticated methods, and a compute-normalized leaderboard would invert much of the field's perceived ranking.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Adaptation methods differ by orders of magnitude in test-time compute, from statistics updates through multi-view augmentation ensembles to iterative optimization per sample, yet leaderboards rank them at unequal compute without normalization.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large part of reported method differences is purchased compute rather than algorithmic insight, so at matched inference budgets, cheap methods plus reinvested compute, such as larger test-time ensembles or bigger backbones, will match or beat expensive adaptation pipelines.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constructing compute-matched frontiers will show simple baselines with reinvested compute dominating a substantial fraction of published methods, reordering the leaderboard particularly at the budget levels edge deployments can afford.
why_important: Adaptation is bought per inference in deployment, and rankings that ignore its price recommend methods practitioners cannot run, while hiding that cheap options may suffice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Compute-normalized comparison is standard in some areas of machine learning; its application to the test-time adaptation literature may be largely absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure per-sample compute of a method panel, define budget tiers, allow every method and baseline the same budget with free reinvestment choices, and re-rank on shifted accuracy per tier.
main_risk: Reinvestment choices for baselines involve design freedom, and unfavorable choices could strawman either side of the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reported accuracy differences are read as algorithmic contributions, with test-time compute treated as an unreported implementation detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some celebrated methods run many forward-backward passes per prediction, a cost that could alternatively fund an ensemble of frozen models, and frozen ensembles are strong robustness baselines.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One expensive adaptation method versus a frozen ensemble sized to its measured compute, one shift battery, compare accuracy at equal cost, one day.

one_line_idea: Generic distribution-divergence measures do not predict transfer performance drop across domains, while cheap hypothesis-disagreement measures do, and the field keeps reporting the wrong quantity.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Papers routinely report input-space or feature-space divergences between domains as evidence of domain gap, implicitly suggesting these numbers relate to how much performance will drop, without validating that relationship.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Task-agnostic divergences correlate weakly with realized accuracy drop because they weight task-irrelevant variation, whereas disagreement between hypotheses trained or probed on the two domains tracks the drop closely, making disagreement the correct reportable statistic.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A meta-evaluation across many domain pairs will show task-agnostic divergence explaining little variance in accuracy drop while classifier-disagreement measures explain most of it, with the gap widest for visually dramatic but task-irrelevant shifts.
why_important: Practitioners triage adaptation effort using gap numbers, and if the standard numbers are uninformative, effort is being allocated by noise.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Theory relating disagreement to transfer exists; a broad empirical meta-evaluation ranking gap measures by predictive validity for modern vision models may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble a large set of domain pairs with measured transfer drops for fixed models, compute a panel of divergence and disagreement measures per pair, and rank measures by explained variance in drop.
main_risk: Disagreement measures need unlabeled target data and a probe-training protocol, and protocol choices could flatter disagreement unless standardized.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Feature-space divergence between domains is treated as a meaningful proxy for expected performance degradation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Divergence sums over all directions of variation while performance depends only on decision-relevant directions, so the correlation between them is structurally unprotected.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Twenty domain pairs, one divergence and one disagreement measure against known drops, compare correlations, one day.

one_line_idea: Classical domain-adaptation generalization bounds are numerically vacuous at foundation scale yet ordinally predictive, and quantifying this rescues theory as a ranking tool.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generalization bounds for domain adaptation involve divergence and capacity terms that evaluate to numbers far above one for deep networks, leading practitioners to dismiss the theory as irrelevant to practice.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Although the bound values are vacuous, their variation across domain pairs and models preserves ordering information, so bound-derived quantities rank transfer difficulty and method suitability nearly as well as expensive empirical trials, making theory useful ordinally where it fails numerically.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across domain-pair and model grids, rank correlation between bound-derived scores and realized transfer performance will be substantially positive and competitive with empirical proxy methods, despite absolute bound values exceeding trivial limits.
why_important: A demonstrated ordinal validity would change how theory is used and taught in this area, from dismissed formalism to cheap decision tool, and would identify which bound terms carry the signal.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Vacuousness of bounds is well known; a systematic ordinal-validity evaluation of bound components at modern scale may be unperformed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute estimable bound components for many domain pairs and models, correlate with realized transfer outcomes, and ablate which components carry ranking power.
main_risk: Bound components must be estimated with their own estimators, and estimator noise could masquerade as theoretical failure or success.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Adaptation theory is regarded as practically inert because its guarantees are numerically meaningless for deep models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Bounds can be loose by a large multiplicative factor and still be monotone in the true quantity, and monotonicity is all that ranking requires.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fifteen domain pairs, one bound-derived score versus realized drops, rank correlation, one day.

one_line_idea: Most accuracy degradation of foundation models under natural shift is captured by a two-parameter description, class-prior change plus uniform margin erosion, enabling label-free degradation forecasting.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Accuracy drops under shift are reported as unstructured numbers per benchmark, without a parsimonious model of how the drop is generated, which blocks extrapolation to unmeasured shifts.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For strong pretrained models, natural shifts act on the output geometry primarily through a shift in effective class priors and a roughly uniform shrinkage of logit margins, so a two-parameter model fit on a small labeled probe predicts full-benchmark degradation curves and per-class error redistribution.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Fitting the two parameters per shift on small probes will reproduce observed accuracy, per-class errors, and confidence histograms on held-out data with small residuals for most natural shifts, while adversarial and correlation-reversal shifts will show large residuals, delimiting the model's scope.
why_important: A validated low-dimensional degradation model turns shift response from a measurement into a forecastable quantity and provides a principled basis for label-free monitoring.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prior-correction and calibration analyses exist separately; a joint minimal parametric account of shift degradation tested for sufficiency across shift families may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For each shift with labels, fit prior-change and margin-shrink parameters on a small subsample, predict aggregate and per-class metrics on the remainder, and quantify residuals by shift family.
main_risk: The two-parameter form may fit accuracy while missing per-class structure, so sufficiency must be tested on distributional metrics, not just the headline number.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Shift degradation is treated as idiosyncratic per benchmark, too heterogeneous for a low-dimensional description.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong models concentrate task information in stable directions, and perturbations of the residual then manifest at the output mostly as noise-like margin loss plus mixture reweighting.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three natural shifts, fit two parameters on ten percent of each, predict accuracy on the rest, check residuals, hours.

one_line_idea: Shift magnitude should be measured in the model's decision-relevant subspace, not in input or generic feature space, and a decision-aware shift norm predicts harm where existing measures fail.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Shift is quantified with input-space or embedding-space statistics that treat all directions equally, while a model's predictions depend on a low-dimensional decision-relevant subspace of its representation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Projecting distributional change onto the decision-relevant subspace, estimated from the model's own head and Jacobians, yields a shift norm that predicts accuracy harm across shift types far better than isotropic measures, and shifts orthogonal to the subspace are certifiably harmless regardless of their isotropic magnitude.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across shifts spanning low-level and semantic changes, the decision-aware norm will dominate isotropic norms in predicting realized harm, and constructed large-magnitude orthogonal shifts will produce near-zero harm as predicted.
why_important: Monitoring keyed to a harm-predictive norm removes false alarms from benign changes and detects small but dangerous changes, which is the core unsolved tradeoff in shift monitoring.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Concentration of decision information is a known phenomenon; an operational decision-aware shift norm validated against harm across shift families may be unbuilt.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate the decision-relevant subspace for fixed models, compute decision-aware and isotropic shift norms across a labeled shift battery, and compare harm-prediction quality, including orthogonal-shift constructions.
main_risk: The decision-relevant subspace estimated on source data may itself rotate under shift, which would erode the norm's validity exactly for severe shifts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Bigger measured distribution change is assumed to mean more risk, with direction treated as unmeasurable detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Harm is mediated entirely by what the decision function reads, so any measure that weights unread directions is measuring something other than risk.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Construct one large orthogonal shift and one small aligned shift for a model, verify the isotropic norm misorders their harm while the decision-aware norm orders correctly, hours.

one_line_idea: Effective-robustness conclusions flip under alternative link functions for the in-distribution-to-shift accuracy relationship, revealing that which models count as robust is partly an artifact of curve-fitting convention.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Effective robustness is defined as residual above a fitted trend relating in-distribution to shifted accuracy across models, with a conventional axis transformation, and residuals near the top of the accuracy range are sensitive to the assumed functional form.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Defensible alternative link functions fit the model population equally well yet assign materially different residuals to individual models, so a subset of published robustness claims about specific models or interventions are artifacts of the conventional form rather than properties of the models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Refitting published model collections under several equally well-fitting link functions will change the sign of estimated effective robustness for a nontrivial fraction of models, concentrated at high accuracy where the transforms diverge most.
why_important: Effective robustness drives claims about which training approaches confer robustness, and form-dependent conclusions require reporting standards that quantify this sensitivity.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The methodology is widely applied; a specification-sensitivity analysis of its conclusions across link functions may be unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit the standard and several alternative link functions to published accuracy pairs, verify comparable goodness of fit, and tabulate sign changes and rank changes of per-model residuals.
main_risk: If one link function fits decisively better, the exercise resolves in favor of a convention and the artifact claim weakens, which is itself a useful result.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The conventional transformation is treated as a settled methodological detail with no bearing on which models are called robust.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Residual-based claims inherit every assumption of the fitted curve, and near accuracy ceilings different monotone transforms reshape residuals dramatically.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One published model collection, refit with two alternative transforms, count residual sign flips among top models, hours.

one_line_idea: Transferability-estimation metrics fail exactly when the probe data is shifted from deployment data, and a shift-aware correction term restores their usefulness for model selection.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Cheap transferability metrics rank candidate pretrained models for a downstream task using a small probe dataset, and practice assumes the probe matches deployment, which is routinely false in shifting environments.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Rankings from existing transferability metrics degrade sharply as probe-to-deployment shift grows, misordering models whose robustness differs, and augmenting the metrics with a term measuring each model's feature stability under the anticipated shift direction restores ranking validity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In a grid of probe-versus-deployment shift severities, standard metrics will show ranking quality decaying with severity, while shift-corrected variants will retain most of their validity, with the largest corrections for models whose in-distribution and shifted behavior diverge.
why_important: Model selection is the highest-leverage decision in applied transfer, and current guidance silently assumes away the shift that most deployments face.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Transferability estimation is an active area; its failure characterization under probe-deployment shift and a corrected estimator may be open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct probe and deployment splits at controlled shift severities, rank model zoos with standard metrics per severity against realized deployment accuracy, and evaluate the corrected estimator on held-out shifts.
main_risk: The correction term needs some characterization of anticipated shift, and if that characterization requires deployment data, the practical advantage narrows.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Transferability scores are treated as intrinsic model-task compatibility measures, robust to where the probe data came from.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The metrics evaluate features on the probe distribution only, so nothing in their construction constrains behavior anywhere else.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One model zoo, one metric, probe on clean data, deploy on corrupted variant, measure ranking-quality drop, one day.

one_line_idea: Enforcing invariance to a nuisance factor provably trades away robustness to shifts correlated with that factor, and the tradeoff is measurable and large in controlled vision experiments.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Invariance to nuisances is pursued as an unqualified good in robust representation learning, yet information removed for invariance is unavailable downstream regardless of whether deployment shifts make it label-relevant.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When a deployment shift changes the relationship between a nuisance factor and labels, models trained invariant to that factor degrade more than non-invariant models, producing a quantifiable invariance-robustness frontier rather than a free lunch.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In controlled setups where a factor is irrelevant at training but becomes label-correlated under shift, invariance-trained models will show degradation exceeding baseline models by a margin growing with enforced invariance strength.
why_important: The result would replace the invariance-is-good heuristic with a quantitative design tradeoff, informing when invariance objectives are safe to deploy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Information-theoretic arguments for this tradeoff exist; controlled empirical frontiers on realistic vision factors may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train models with graded invariance penalties on a chosen factor, construct test shifts where that factor gains label relevance, and map degradation versus invariance strength against matched shifts where the factor stays irrelevant.
main_risk: Constructing shifts where a factor becomes relevant without changing other statistics requires careful synthetic or semi-synthetic design, limiting immediate external validity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Invariance to nuisances is assumed to weakly dominate, helping under relevant shifts and costing nothing otherwise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deleted information cannot be conditionally recovered, and deployment gets no vote in what training deleted, so the cost side of the ledger is structural.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train with and without invariance to color on a task where color is spurious, test on a shift making color informative, compare drops, one day.

one_line_idea: Importance weighting for covariate shift, long dismissed as hopeless in high dimensions, becomes practical when density ratios are estimated in foundation-model embedding space.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Importance-weighted correction for covariate shift is theoretically principled but was largely abandoned for images because density-ratio estimation in pixel space is intractable and weights explode in high dimensions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation embeddings compress shift-relevant variation into low effective dimension where density ratios are estimable with controlled variance, so embedding-space importance weighting delivers reliable covariate-shift correction for reweighting evaluation and fine-tuning, reviving a method the field wrote off.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On benchmark covariate shifts, embedding-space ratio estimators will produce stable weights with bounded effective-sample-size loss and yield accuracy and evaluation-estimate improvements over unweighted baselines, where pixel-space estimation fails outright.
why_important: Working importance weights unlock unbiased offline evaluation under shift and principled reweighted training, tools currently unavailable to vision practitioners.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Density-ratio estimation theory is mature; a systematic revival study establishing where embedding-space weighting works, with variance diagnostics, may be unwritten.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate ratios in frozen embedding space across shift benchmarks, diagnose weight variance and effective sample size, and test downstream utility in weighted evaluation against labeled ground truth.
main_risk: Embedding compression may discard shift-relevant directions, biasing ratios in ways that are invisible without labels, so bias diagnostics are as important as variance control.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Importance weighting is considered a textbook method that does not survive contact with image data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The dismissal was earned in pixel space, and the dimensionality argument against it weakens by orders of magnitude in a semantic embedding.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One shift pair, logistic-regression ratio estimation on embeddings, check weight stability and weighted-evaluation error against labels, hours.

one_line_idea: Language is an adaptation surface: systematic per-domain prompt construction matches gradient-based adaptation of vision-language models at a tiny fraction of the cost and risk.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-language models expose a text interface that changes the classifier without touching weights, and adaptation research nevertheless concentrates on gradient-based updates whose cost and risk block deployment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For a broad class of deployment shifts, the accuracy recoverable by any unsupervised adaptation is largely recoverable by domain-conditioned prompt construction alone, generated by a fixed systematic procedure from a short domain characterization, because the text tower already encodes the needed domain priors.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across shift benchmarks, procedurally generated domain-conditioned prompts will close a fraction of the shift gap comparable to unsupervised gradient methods, with complementary gains when combined, and near-zero variance across reruns since nothing is trained.
why_important: A no-training adaptation path changes the deployment calculus entirely, especially for edge and regulated settings where weight updates are prohibited.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt sensitivity is well known; a rigorous equivalence study between systematic prompt-space adaptation and gradient-space adaptation under matched information may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a fixed prompt-construction procedure taking a domain description, compare its gap closure against gradient-based adaptation across shifts on the same backbone, and test the combination.
main_risk: Procedure design could covertly overfit to benchmark domains, so the procedure must be frozen before evaluation and tested on held-out shift types.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Prompt adjustments are considered cosmetic relative to weight adaptation, which is treated as the substantive mechanism.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The classifier of a vision-language model literally is the text embedding, so rewriting the text is a direct parameterization of the decision boundary, not a cosmetic change.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three shifts, fixed prompt template family conditioned on one-sentence domain descriptions versus one gradient method, compare gap closure, hours.

one_line_idea: The text tower has its own distribution-shift problem: class-name register, dialect, and terminology shifts degrade vision-language classification as much as image shifts, and no benchmark measures this axis.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Zero-shot classifiers are built from class names embedded by the text tower, and deployed vocabularies differ from benchmark vocabularies by region, profession, register, and language, while robustness evaluation varies only the images.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Semantically equivalent but lexically shifted class vocabularies induce accuracy drops comparable in magnitude to standard image shifts, with the damage concentrated in classes whose common names diverge from web-caption conventions, constituting an unmeasured second axis of shift.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating fixed models on fixed images while systematically shifting class vocabularies through synonyms, regional terms, and professional terminology will produce accuracy distributions whose spread rivals the spread across standard image-shift benchmarks.
why_important: Real deployments choose their own vocabularies, and if lexical choice moves accuracy as much as image distribution does, current robustness certification misses half the risk surface.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Prompt sensitivity is documented for templates; a systematic characterization of class-name distribution shift as a robustness axis with severity-controlled lexical perturbations may be absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build vocabulary variants of standard label sets with verified semantic equivalence, evaluate fixed models across variants on unchanged images, and compare the induced accuracy spread against image-shift spreads.
main_risk: Ensuring semantic equivalence of vocabulary variants requires careful validation, since accidental meaning drift would inflate the measured effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Class names are treated as fixed inputs of the task rather than a distribution that shifts across deployments.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The text tower was trained on web caption conventions, and any vocabulary drawn from a different linguistic distribution is out-of-distribution input to half of the model.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One label set, three semantically verified vocabulary variants, one model, compare accuracy spread to one image-corruption severity step, hours.

one_line_idea: Under image distribution shift, vision-language assistants lean harder on language priors, so their accuracy degrades gracefully while their visual grounding collapses, and accuracy-only evaluation hides the swap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multimodal assistants can answer many visual questions from linguistic plausibility alone, and shift evaluations of such systems report answer accuracy without measuring whether answers remain grounded in the image.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] As image quality or distribution degrades, these systems substitute language-prior guessing for visual evidence, so measured accuracy declines slowly while grounding metrics, such as consistency with image-specific perturbations, decline steeply, meaning robustness claims based on accuracy measure prior strength rather than perception.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Jointly tracking accuracy and grounding diagnostics across shift severity will show the two curves diverging, with grounding falling substantially before accuracy does, and the divergence largest on questions with strong linguistic priors.
why_important: A system that keeps answering plausibly while no longer seeing is more dangerous than one that visibly fails, since downstream users cannot detect the substitution.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Language-prior reliance is documented in visual question answering; its interaction with distribution shift as a robustness measurement problem may be uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct shifted variants of visual question sets, measure accuracy alongside grounding probes such as answer sensitivity to image-content edits, and compare degradation curves across severity.
main_risk: Grounding diagnostics are imperfect proxies, and probe artifacts could exaggerate the divergence unless multiple independent grounding measures agree.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Slow accuracy degradation of multimodal assistants under shift is read as evidence of robust visual understanding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The language prior is shift-invariant by construction, so any degradation of the visual channel mechanically increases the prior's share of the answer without necessarily moving accuracy on prior-aligned questions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One assistant, one question set at two corruption severities, measure accuracy and answer-flip rate under content-changing edits, compare divergence, one day.

one_line_idea: The caption-style provenance of pretraining data determines which visual shifts a vision-language model is robust to, giving each model a predictable robustness fingerprint.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision-language models are trained on caption distributions that differ in provenance, from alt-text through curated descriptions to synthetic captions, and robustness differences between models are usually attributed to scale or architecture without examining caption provenance.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Caption provenance controls which visual variations pretraining associates with stable semantics, so models trained with different caption styles will exhibit systematically different per-shift-family robustness profiles, predictable from measurable properties of their caption distributions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing models matched in scale but differing in caption provenance will reveal reproducible profile differences, such as synthetic-caption models showing different robustness to context and attribute shifts, with profile features traceable to caption statistics like attribute mention rates.
why_important: If robustness fingerprints are predictable from caption statistics, data builders gain a lever to engineer robustness before training rather than discovering it after.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Caption quality effects on aggregate accuracy are studied; provenance-to-robustness-profile mapping across shift families may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or obtain scale-matched models differing mainly in caption provenance, evaluate across a shift-family battery, and correlate profile differences with measured caption-distribution statistics.
main_risk: Truly caption-only-different model pairs are rare, and image-distribution differences between training sets could confound the attribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Robustness differences among vision-language models are attributed to data scale and model size, with caption style treated as a quality knob for accuracy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Captions define which image variations map to the same text targets, and that mapping is the supervision signal from which invariances are learned.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two public models differing in caption pipeline, evaluate on two contrasting shift families, check for profile crossover, one day.

one_line_idea: Cross-modal agreement between image and text pathways is a label-free estimator of shift harm specific to vision-language models, outperforming confidence-based estimators.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Estimating performance degradation without labels is a core monitoring need, and existing estimators rely on the model's confidence, which shifts corrupt; vision-language models uniquely possess two semi-independent pathways whose agreement is observable.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Degradation of the visual pathway under shift breaks its agreement with text-side expectations in measurable ways, so agreement statistics between image embeddings and text-anchored structure estimate accuracy loss more reliably than confidence-based methods, because the text side provides a shift-stable reference.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across shift families with labeled ground truth, cross-modal agreement statistics will predict realized accuracy drops with lower error than confidence-based estimators, especially on semantic shifts where confidence-based methods are known to fail.
why_important: A more reliable label-free harm estimator directly upgrades every monitoring pipeline built on vision-language models, which are becoming the default deployed vision stack.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Modality-gap phenomena are studied descriptively; exploiting cross-modal agreement as a quantitative accuracy-drop estimator benchmarked against the estimation literature may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define agreement statistics from image-text embedding geometry, evaluate their accuracy-drop prediction across a labeled shift battery, and benchmark against established confidence-based estimators on identical data.
main_risk: Shifts that damage both pathways coherently, or that originate in the text side, would break the stable-reference assumption underlying the estimator.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Performance estimation under shift is approached through the output distribution, treating the model as a single opaque predictor.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Two measurements with partially independent failure modes support consistency checking that no single-pathway statistic can provide, a standard redundancy argument applied to multimodal structure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three shifts with labels, one agreement statistic versus one confidence-based estimator, compare drop-prediction errors, hours.

one_line_idea: Generative vision models used as classifiers have a qualitatively different distribution-shift robustness profile than discriminative foundation models, defining an unexplored complementary paradigm.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Classification can be performed by scoring class-conditional generation or reconstruction under generative models, and robustness evaluation practice is built almost entirely around discriminative architectures and their failure modes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Generative classification degrades under different shift families than discriminative classification, being more stable under low-level and style shifts that preserve generability while failing differently under semantic novelty, so the two paradigms have complementary robustness profiles exploitable by simple combination.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Matched evaluation of generative and discriminative classification across shift families will show low correlation between their per-shift degradation patterns, and an agreement-gated combination will exceed either alone on worst-case-across-shifts performance.
why_important: If the paradigms fail differently, robustness-critical systems gain diversity from paradigm mixing that no amount of discriminative ensembling provides.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Generative classifiers are studied for accuracy and adversarial robustness; a systematic natural-shift profile comparison against discriminative foundation models may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement generative classification with a public generative model, evaluate alongside a discriminative model on a matched shift battery, compare per-family degradation correlations, and test the gated combination.
main_risk: Generative classification is computationally heavy and sensitive to scoring design choices, and a weak scoring implementation could misrepresent the paradigm.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Discriminative models are treated as the only serious classification paradigm, with generative scoring seen as an inefficient curiosity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The two paradigms consume different sufficient statistics of the image, so shifts that destroy one's evidence can leave the other's intact, which is the precondition for complementary failure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One generative and one discriminative model, classification on two contrasting shift types, compare which degrades where, one day.
